title: Oral Presentation
paragraphs: Background: Maternal gut microbiota plays a critical role in establishing the infant gut microbiome, which influences long-term metabolic and immune health. Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is known to alter maternal gut microbiota, but its impact on vertical transmission to infants remains inadequately explored. Methods: We conducted a single-centre prospective cohort study involving 29 mother–infant dyads affected by GDM and 22 healthy control dyads. Stool samples were collected from mothers (third trimester), infant meconium (at birth), and infant stool at six weeks of age. Gut microbiome profiling was performed using targeted 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing (V3–V4 region). Microbiome analysis included PERMANOVA to assess global compositional differences, differential abundance testing, and functional prediction using PICRUSt2 to identify GDM-associated taxa and their vertical transfer patterns. Results: Mothers with GDM showed significantly altered gut microbiota compared to controls (PERMANOVA, P < 0.05), with enrichment of pro-inflammatory and metabolically active genera such as Collinsella , Blautia , and Ruminococcus . Infants of GDM mothers demonstrated distinct gut microbiome profiles at birth and at six weeks, compared to control infants at the same time points (PERMANOVA, p.adjusted < 0.05). Notably, Blautia and Collinsella —genera enriched in GDM mothers—were also detected in their infants, suggesting potential vertical transmission. Additionally, an adverse maternal microbiome was associated with poorer OGTT responses in GDM mothers ( P < 0.05) and, in a subset of infants ( n = 11) of GDM mothers, correlated with lower BMI Z-scores at 12-month follow-up. Conclusion: Our findings provide the first Indian evidence that GDM significantly disrupts maternal gut microbiota and alters infant gut colonization via vertical transmission. This dysbiosis in infants may increase susceptibility to future metabolic and inflammatory disorders in later life, emphasizing the importance of optimizing maternal metabolic health during pregnancy.

Background: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune disorder marked by the destruction of pancreatic beta-cells, leading to insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility, particularly within the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) region, plays a major role. Data on HLA associations in South Indian populations remain limited, and region-specific insights are essential for improving early diagnosis and personalized interventions. Methods: A cross-sectional observational study was conducted at Gandhi Medical College and Hospital, Secunderabad, from August 2022 to August 2024. Fifty-seven T1DM patients and their non-diabetic siblings were recruited. Clinical evaluations, autoantibody tests (GAD65, IA-2), and biochemical analyses were conducted. High-resolution HLA genotyping for Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) and Class II (HLA-DRB1, -DQA1, -DQB1) alleles was performed using next-generation sequencing. Statistical tests included Fisher’s exact test, odds ratios, and Bonferroni correction. Results: Risk alleles associated with T1DM included HLA-A*02, A*11, B*40, C*12, DRB1*03, DPB1*04/14, and DQB1*02/03. Protective alleles included A*24, B*35, C*07, DRB1*07, DPB1*02/15, and DQB1*05/06. Significant haplotypes such as DRB1*03-DQB1*02 and A*02-B*40-C*03-DRB1*04-DQB1*03 were identified. Autoantibody positivity was linked to specific HLA profiles. Conclusion: This is the first high-resolution HLA genotyping study using NGS in South Indian T1DM patients. The findings reveal distinct genetic risk and protective markers, supporting the inclusion of HLA screening in T1DM risk assessment and personalized care.

Background: SA have a higher risk of GDM even at lower levels of obesity. Hyperactive HPA with altered diurnal cortisol rhythms have been observed in metabolic syndrome, obesity and diabetes. We hypothesised that differences in HPA activity could explain increased risk of GDM in SA. Methods: A prospective multicentre study of high-risk SA and WC women (PRiDE-HPA study). Subjects: SA and WC women, <16 weeks of gestation, meeting selective screening criteria for GDM, after excluding steroid use and multiple pregnancy. Saliva collected at waking, 30 min after, 4 pmd and bedtime twice in pregnancy (12 and 24 weeks) for cortisol and cortisone. At OGTT fasting (FPG), 1 and 2 h plasma glucose was estimated. 24 h urine was collected for Glucocorticoid metabolites. The differences in salivary and urinary GC metabolites were studied in SA and WC in relation to glycaemia in pregnancy. Results: CAR (cortisone awakening response) was higher in SA after adjusting for Ethnicity, gestational age, waking time, smoking (B = 0.401 (0.031, 0.771), P = 0.034). SA had significantly higher HSD2 (-0.069 (-0.137, -0.002), P = 0.045) and lower total HSD activity (-0.162 (-0.230, -0.094), P < 0.0001) to WC. Waking and peak cortisone in early pregnancy correlated independently with FPG at 24 weeks in both ethnicities (B = 1.469 (0.256, 2.681), P = 0.019 and 0.591 (0.04, 1.13), P = 0.035). While BMI was an independent predictor of total GC excretion in WC, adiposity but not BMI independently predicted total glucocorticoid excretion in SA. Conclusion: Differences in HPA activity and cortisol clearance could explain the higher risk of GDM in SA. Early pregnancy waking salivary cortisone was an independent predictor of glycaemia in later pregnancy and could be used as an early predictor of GDM.

Background: There is lack of data on clinical outcomes of structured care model for Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) at secondary care level in lower-middle income countries. With help from Government of West Bengal, India, a structured care model for T1D was implemented wherein model clinics were established in district hospitals. Objectives: To evaluate impact of government-supported structured care model implemented in district hospitals on clinical parameters of children and adolescents living with T1D in West Bengal, India, over a 24-month period. Methods: Longitudinal multi-center study was conducted among T1D subjects who were enrolled in model government-funded clinics in five district hospitals in West Bengal. Clinical parameters were evaluated at baseline, at 12 months, and at 24 months following implementation of model. Results: Study included 366 T1D subjects, mean age: 15.4 ± 6.7 years, age at diagnosis: 8.7 ± 4.9 years. 41.4% belonged to lower socioeconomic class and most parents/caregivers had not completed primary education. Immediately upon enrolment in the model, all subjects were transitioned to basal-bolus insulin regimen. At two years, study drop-out rate was zero and subjects were followed up 23.5 times in 24 months. Mean ± SD glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) reduced significantly from 10.0 ± 2.7% (86 ± 30 mmol/mol) at baseline to 9.1 ± 2.4% (76 ± 26 mmol/mol) at one year, and to 8.5 ± 1.9% (70 ± 21 mmol/mol) at two years ( P < 0.01). There were no episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis, hospital admissions or deaths, during the study period. Conclusion: Findings provide evidence that structured care can be delivered in lower-middle income countries by government-funded model including establishment of clinics within secondary-level district hospitals.

Background: Post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM) is a common metabolic complication following renal transplantation, largely attributed to immunosuppressive therapy particularly calcineurin inhibitors and corticosteroids. Transient hyperglycemia is frequently observed in the immediate post-operative period due to surgical stress and high-dose corticosteroids; therefore, PTDM diagnosis is typically established after stabilization of immunosuppressive regimens, around 6 weeks post-transplant. Objective : To determine the incidence and identify predictors of PTDM in renal transplant recipients at a tertiary care center in South India. Methods: This was a retrospective and prospective observational study involving 100 non-diabetic chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients who underwent renal transplantation and were followed for 6 months. PTDM was diagnosed based on American Diabetes Association (ADA) criteria using fasting blood glucose, random blood glucose, and HbA1c measurements. Demographic and clinical parameters were compared between PTDM and non-PTDM groups. Results: The study included 73% males (mean age: 38.78 ± 10.26 years) and 27% females (mean age: 37.78 ± 12.23 years), with 90% of patients residing in southern India. PTDM incidence was 3% at 6 weeks, 7% at 3 months, and 23% at 6 months. Significant predictors included:

At 6 months, 73.9% of PTDM patients were on oral hypoglycemics, 4% on insulin, and 2% on both. PTDM patients had a significantly higher infection rate (14.4% vs 3.9%, P = 0.047). No statistically significant differences were observed in age, gender, post-operative hyperglycemia, cumulative steroid dose, etiology of CKD, or donor type. Conclusion: This study highlights a high incidence of PTDM (23%) within first 6 months following renal transplantation. Important risk factors were family history of diabetes, higher pre-transplant body weight, elevated BMI, and higher tacrolimus levels at 1 month. Among these, body weight is a modifiable risk factor. Early detection of high-risk patients and effective management of PTDM can reduce the complications of PTDM, such as infections and cardio-vascular events.

Background: Fibrocalculous Pancreatic Diabetes (FCPD) is a distinct and severe form of diabetes resulting from Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis (TCP), commonly seen in tropical regions. It differs from other types of diabetes due to its early onset, association with pancreatic calcification, and genetic predisposition, particularly SPINK1 mutations. FCPD typically requires early insulin initiation, enzyme replacement therapy, and routine screening for pancreatic cancer. Historically, it was believed that diabetes-related complications were less common in secondary forms like FCPD, but comparative data, especially with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM), remain limited. Objectives: To evaluate the prevalence of microvascular complications in patients with FCPD and compare them with those in T1DM patients. Methods: This prospective cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary care center. Thirty-six FCPD patients were recruited along with age- and gender-matched T1DM patients. Neuropathy was assessed using the Neuropathy Symptom Score, Neuropathy Disability Score, and monofilament test. Retinopathy was evaluated through dilated fundus examination using +90 diopter biomicroscopy. Nephropathy was assessed using albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR <60 mL/min). Results: The mean age at onset was 31 years for FCPD and 17 years for T1DM. Seventeen FCPD patients reported steatorrhea; one had night blindness. The prevalence of microvascular complications was comparable: neuropathy (22% FCPD vs 10.5% T1DM, P = 0.3), nephropathy (43% vs 21%, P = 0.12), and retinopathy (2.8% vs 5.3%, P = 0.6). Conclusion: FCPD patients demonstrate a similar prevalence of microvascular complications as those with T1DM, challenging earlier assumptions and highlighting the importance of early screening and consistent follow-up in FCPD management.

Background: Nocturnal hypoglycemia is a life-threatening yet underappreciated complication in patients with brittle diabetes, such as Fibrocalcific Pancreatic Diabetes (FCPD). Advanced prediction of nocturnal hypoglycemia using artificial intelligence (AI), combined with timely preventive interventions, may help mitigate nighttime risk and improve patient safety. Methods: We developed an Evidential Neural Network (ENN)-based model, NIDRA-HYPO, to predict overnight minimum glucose levels and the risk of nocturnal hypoglycemia before bedtime in individuals with FCPD. The model was trained on data from 50 FCPD patients under free-living conditions, comprising over 10,000 nocturnal data points. Inputs included continuous glucose monitoring (Libre FGMS), insulin dosing, physical activity (tracked using Fitbit Inspire 3), and meal-related information. A decision-theoretic criterion was applied to determine the optimal glucose threshold for identifying hypoglycemia risk, maximizing expected net benefit. Model performance was evaluated on an independent validation cohort of 11 FCPD patients over a 4-week period, also under free-living conditions while on multiple daily insulin (MDI) therapy. Primary outcome measures included sensitivity and specificity of hypoglycemia prediction, correlation between predicted and actual minimum nocturnal glucose levels, and root-mean-square error (RMSE). The model was further tested for its preventive capability through risk-based intelligent-snacks recommendation based on AI derived threshold. Results: The model predicted 93.7% of nocturnal hypoglycemia events (<70 mg/dL; 95% CI, 70.9–99.2) with an AUC of 0.84 (95% CI, 0.76–0.94), 0–4 h prior to sleep. The correlation between predicted and actual minimum glucose was strong ( R = 0.74, P < 0.001). In the validation cohort, the model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 ( P = 0.001). The intelligent-snack intervention significantly reduced both the frequency and duration of nocturnal hypoglycemia ( P < 0.001) without affecting time-in-range. Conclusion: This study validates the first ENN-integrated decision support tool for FCPD, offering a novel approach to predicting and preventing nocturnal hypoglycemia through proactive AI empowered carbohydrate recommendations.

Background: Renal dysfunction in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) can be because of diabetes itself, known as diabetic kidney disease (DKD), or due to other aetiology, termed non-diabetic kidney disease (NDKD). Current clinical, biochemical, and radiological parameters are unable to distinguish DKD from NDKD, making renal biopsy the gold standard. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play crucial roles in gene regulation and cellular processes. Animal/cell model studies have suggested that several miRNAs are dysregulated in DKD but their role in humans with biopsy proven kidney disease remains unexplored. Aim: To identify differentially expressed miRNAs capable of differentiating DKD from NDKD in T2DM patients. Method: A total of 120 participants were enrolled: 30 biopsy-confirmed DKD, 30 biopsy-confirmed NDKD, 30 T2DM without kidney disease (T2DM control), and 30 healthy controls. miRNAs were selected via literature and database mining. Urine (second morning sample) and plasma were collected in fasting state. Total RNA was extracted and miRNA expression profiled using quantitative real-time PCR in urinary cell and plasma derived RNA. Results: 9 candidate miRNAs (hsa-let-7c-5p, miR-200a-3p, miR-200c-3p, miR-203a-3p, miR-216a-5p, miR-143-3p, miR-106b-5p, miR-214-3p, and miR-106a-5p) were shortlisted. In urinary cell-derived RNA, miR-216a-5p, miR-214-3p, and miR-200c-3p were significantly deregulated in DKD compared to T2DM, while let-7c-5p and miR-200c-3p showed differential expression between DKD and NDKD. In plasma, only miR-203a-3p was upregulated in DKD in comparison to T2DM. Importantly, miR-216a-5p, miR-214-3p, miR-200c-3p, and let-7c-5p showed statistically significant alterations only in urinary cell derived RNA samples, but not in plasma-derived RNA, suggesting that these miRNAs may be specifically associated with kidney pathology. Conclusion: This study shows that urinary miRNAs could potentially help to differentiate DKD from NDKD and may help in preselect patients who (NDKD) truly need a biopsy for accurate diagnosis and treatment.

Background: Nailfold videocapillaroscopy (NFC) is a novel, non-invasive technique to assess microvascular alterations in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Chronic hyperglycemia contributes to microvascular damage, reflected in capillary morphological changes. This interim analysis evaluates NFC parameter changes in relation to diabetic retinopathy (DR) in T2DM. Methods: Patients with T2DM attending the endocrinology clinic at St. John’s Medical College, Bengaluru were enrolled. All patients underwent fundus evaluation for presence of DR. NFC was performed using standard protocol, assessing five quantitative parameters, which were compared between DR and non-DR groups. Results: The study included 70 patients (23 females, 47 males), with a mean age of 52.0 ± 8.0 years and mean diabetes duration of 8.7 ± 6.0 years. Of these, 15 had DR and 55 did not. The mean HbA1c among patients with DR was 9.47 ± 2.04%, while in those without DR it was 7.61 ± 1.31%. Compared to patients without DR, those with DR demonstrated the following NFC changes: capillary density was reduced (mean: 6.6 ± 0.7/mm vs. 8.4 ± 0.8/mm), capillary length decreased (mean: 190 ± 25 vs. 260 ± 30 µm), intercapillary distance increased (mean: 190 ± 35 µm vs. 140 ± 25 µm), capillary width increased (mean: 27 ± 5 µm vs. 18 ± 4 µm), and capillary loop diameter was larger (mean: 28 ± 3 µm vs. 18 ± 2.5 µm). Conclusion: Nailfold videocapillaroscopy reveals distinct microvascular abnormalities in T2DM patients with DR. NFC may serve as a simple, non-invasive tool for early detection of microvascular complications in T2DM, potentially guiding timely interventions.

Background: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) affects nearly 48.4% of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients in India and remains a major cause of chronic kidney failure requiring renal replacement therapy. Albuminuria is a key marker of DKD progression. Inflammation is central to DKD pathogenesis. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), known for its anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing effects, may offer renal protection. Methods: This open-label randomized controlled trial included 40 adults above 18 years of age with T2DM (HbA1c 7–10%), macroalbuminuria (UACR ≥300 mg/g), and eGFR 30–90 mL/min/1.73 m². Patients were randomized into two groups: HCQ (up to 400 mg/day) plus standard therapy ( n = 20), and standard therapy alone ( n = 20). Patients on SGLT2 inhibitors continued them. Primary outcomes were changes in urinary albumin creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) over a 3-month period. Results: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. Mean UACR at baseline was 4542.69 mg/g in the intervention group and 4523.62 mg/g in the control group. Mean eGFR was 51.41 and 57.78 mL/min/1.73 m², respectively. After 3 months, the intervention group showed a significant 41.44% reduction in UACR ( P < 0.05), suggesting a beneficial renal effect. A 1.7% decline in eGFR in the intervention group was not statistically significant, indicating preserved renal function. Conclusion: Hydroxychloroquine, when added to standard therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established diabetic kidney disease, significantly reduced albuminuria over a 3-month period without adversely affecting eGFR. These findings suggest a potential renoprotective role of HCQ in slowing DKD progression, warranting larger and longer-duration studies to validate its efficacy and safety.

Background: In women, the evidences regarding the association between diabetes and sexual dysfunction are less conclusive as compared to males. Diabetes-induced vascular and nerve dysfunctions may impair the sexual response by producing structural and functional changes in the female genitalia. The present study is significant in this regard that it has been conducted among individuals hailing from urban, suburban and rural areas of the state of West Bengal making questionnaires in vernacular languages to reach maximum number of individuals possible. The data obtained was analysed statistically to derive conclusions. Methods: In this cross-: Sectional 100 female patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus attending the diabetes clinic in Endocrine OPD, were screened and included as the study population. Sexual dysfunctions in women was measured here using the standard questionnaire and the FSFI score <24 was taken as the criteria for accepting the presence of sexual dysfunction. The FSD score was compared against parameters like age, duration of diabetes, Body mass index (BMI), blood sugar (glycemic status) fasting and post-prandial, diabetes-related complications and addiction and prevalence was calculated. Results: Prevalence of sexual dysfunction in the study population is 51% showing association between diabetes and female sexual dysfunction. The prevalence of FSD was found to be maximum (75%) in the age group 41-50 years. Strong association of FSD with age is found as P -value is 0.002. the prevalence of FSD was maximum (92.31%) in the participants whose Duration of diabetes more than equal to 11 years. Very Strong association of FSD with Duration of diabetes is found as P -value < 0.001. The prevalence of FSD was found to be maximum (94.74%) in the group (19% of the study population) who are on insulin. Extremely strong association of FSD with insulin usage is found as P -value is 0.000. The prevalence of FSD was found to be maximum (71.43%) in the group (42% of the study population) who do not have controlled ppbg (>180 mg/dl). Quite strong association of FSD with ppbg control is found as P -value is 0.001. The prevalence of FSD was found to be maximum (72.5%) in the participants who were overweight. 11% of the population is obese and in them prevalence of FSD is 63.64. Very strong association of FSD with BMI of the participant is found as p-value is 0.000. Major association of FSD was seen absent with addiction, OHA intake, micro and macrovascular compications in the patients. Of all the six domains evaluated to reach FSFI score, majority of the patients had decreased desire. Prevalence Conclusion: Of sexual dysfunction in the study population is 51%. Longer duration of diabetes, inadequate diabetes control, insulin intake, obesity (higher BMI) and higher age of the participant has a role to play in the development of FSD as per this study. The ability to diagnose and treat FSD in unsuspecting diabetics will result in long term improvement in quality of life.

Background: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) manifests as albuminuric and non-albuminuric phenotypes with distinct clinical and pathological characteristics. A significant knowledge gap exists in comparing their urinary proteomic profiles, particularly in prospectively performed biopsy-proven DKD. Identification of a unique proteome signature would help to differentiate between phenotypes and understand the pathogenesis of DKD. Method: Patients with type 2 diabetes and suspected DKD aged > 18 years with renal insufficiency (eGFR of 30-60 ml/min/m 2 ) who were not yet on SGLT2i, RAASi and MRAs underwent biopsy. Individuals with non-diabetic kidney disease or mixed pathology were excluded. Clinical and histopathological data were collected and compared. Urine samples were collected from 33 biopsy-proven DKD patients (20 albuminuric, 13 non-albuminuric), along with control groups (Healthy and T2DM). Urinary proteins were isolated and analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Protein identification was performed using Proteome Discoverer against the Uniprot database. Appropriate bioinformatics analysis was performed to identify unique protein signatures distinguishing the two DKD groups. Results : Albuminuric DKD subjects showed higher prevalence of neuropathy (90% vs 54%, P = 0.03) and retinopathy (85% vs 46%, P = 0.007), with elevated HDL levels ( P = 0.005) as compared to non-albuminuric DKD. Histologically, they showed advanced DKD (mainly RPS 3, KW lesions, and Mesangial matrix expansion), while non-albuminuric DKD had milder glomerular changes (RPS 1/2a). Urinary proteome analysis revealed one protein was exclusive to albuminuric DKD, while three unique proteins were identified in non-albuminuric DKD. Conclusion: Albuminuric DKD demonstrated higher incidence of neuropathy, retinopathy, elevated HDL, and advanced glomerular lesions compared to non-albuminuric DKD. These two phenotypes may have some unique urinary proteome profile which needs to be tested in future prospective studies for clinical implementation.

Background: Short stature resulting from growth hormone (GH)–insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) axis dysregulation encompasses a spectrum of disorders with diverse clinical and genetic etiologies. Identifying the underlying cause is crucial for effective intervention. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical, radiological, hormonal, and genetic profiles of children with proportionate short stature related to GH-IGF1 axis abnormalities. Methods: This retrospective, cross-sectional study was conducted at the Department of Endocrinology, Gandhi Medical College, Musheerabad. A total of 30 children with proportionate short stature and suspected GH-IGF1 axis disorders were included. Data were collected from medical records, including clinical parameters, GH stimulation test results, IGF1 levels, brain MRI findings, and genetic analyses through targeted panels and exome sequencing. Results: Among the 30 patients (16 males, 14 females; mean age: 9.35 years), 24 were diagnosed with isolated GH deficiency (IGHD). Genetic causes included 7 with GHRHR mutations, 1 with GH1 mutation (bioinactive GH), 1 with LTBP3 mutation, 1 with WDR4/LARP7 mutations, and 1 with LHX3 mutation. Structural abnormalities were observed in 6 cases of pituitary stalk interruption syndrome (3 IGHD, 3 MPHD), 1 case of septo-optic dysplasia, and 2 cases of ectopic thyroid with CFTR mutations. One patient had GH insensitivity and one had MPHD with anterior pituitary hypoplasia. Notably, 18 of the 30 patients showed greater compromise in weight age than height age, suggesting undernutrition. This highlights that GHD should still be investigated even in resource-limited settings where nutritional stunting may coexist. Conclusion: GH-IGF1 axis disorders in short stature present with substantial clinical and genetic heterogeneity. GHRHR mutations were the most frequent genetic finding. Weight deficits were more pronounced than height deficits in many patients, suggesting undernutrition as a coexisting factor. However, this should not preclude the investigation for GH deficiency. Comprehensive hormonal, radiological, and genetic assessments are crucial for accurate diagnosis and individualized management.

Background: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) for pituitary hormones and transcription factors (TFs) on tumour tissue can identify hormone positive Silent Pituitary Adenoma (SPA) and true null cell adenomas-NCA (negative for both hormone and TFs) which have poorer prognosis. Aims and Objectives: To assess prevalence of SPA and especially null cell adenomas. Methods: IHC for pituitary hormone GH, PRL, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH and TFs like SF1 and PIT1, T-PIT was performed on available tumour samples for patients who underwent surgery from January 2020-December 2024. Clinical data, investigations including radiology perimetry and follow up was recorded on predesigned proforma. Results: Out of 493 patients of pituitary adenoma enrolled, 266 patients (median age of 45.5, range-18-69 years, Males:166) were diagnosed with SPA and 165 have been operated. IHC was diffusely positive(cytoplasmic) for ACTH in 32, GH-15, prolactin-19, TSH-30 and FSH/LH in 40 and diffuse positivity(nuclear) was seen for PIT1 in 76, SF1-70 and T-PIT in 4 specimens. In this study,17 had NCA [(Males-7 age (26-71) years-median age 45 years)]. All had headache with 11 having bilateral visual loss with bitemporal hemianopia. MRI showed Knosp grading (invasive-3/4) in 13 patients with median diameter of 3.3cm. Average duration of disease was 2.5 years, two of them expired in post-op period. Two patients had persistent tumours after 12 months, one went for radiotherapy, one for cabergoline. The demographic, clinical and biochemical parameters were not statistically different between who were IHC positive for hormones/TFs and those who were negative. Conclusion: Prevalence of NCA in our series was 6.3% which is higher than that reported in literature (1%).

This work is supported by the Council of Science & Technology, UP, Lucknow research project titled “Pathological classification and Clinical outcomes of Silent (Non-functioning) Pituitary Adenomas” (Project ID:1599) and other funding agency Endocrine Society of India (ESIRG-24-49).

Objective: Radiotherapy (RT) is an established second-line treatment in adult Cushing disease (CD). However, data regarding pituitary RT in pediatric CD is scarce. This study aims to demonstrate the effectiveness and long-term safety of fractionated conformal-RT (CRT) in pediatric and adolescent CD patients. Methods: This single-centre retrospective study included thirty-four out of 108 pediatric patients with CD (≤20 years at presentation) who underwent first/second/third-line CRT between 1994-2024, with a minimum one-year follow-up post-CRT. Results: Data of 34 CD patients (21 males, 07 prepubertal, 24 microadenomas) with post-CRT median follow-up of 74.5 (34.5-127.3) months were analyzed. Post-CRT, 25/34 (73.5%) patients achieved remission at 16.5 (8.75-39.25) months. Younger age at CD diagnosis (13.4 vs. 19.0 years, P = 0.01) and CRT post-first-TSS vs. post-second-TSS (remission rate: 93.8 vs. 53.8%; P = 0.026) predicted remission. In the multivariate Cox proportional hazards model, only younger age at CD diagnosis was significantly associated with a higher likelihood of remission over time (HR: 0.795, 95% CI: 0.665–0.951, P = 0.012). Ketoconazole use predicted relapse post-CRT remission (log-rank test, P = 0.006). Growth hormone deficiency occurred in 17/20 (85%), while 29/34 (41.4%) patients had low IGF-1 levels. New-onset hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (HH) and central hypothyroidism (CHT) occurred in 3/24 (12.5%) and 4/24 (16.7%) patients, respectively. Older age at CD diagnosis (17.5 vs. 13.0 years; P = 0.04) and at CRT administration (23 vs. 14 years; P = 0.03) predicted new-onset HH or CHT post-CRT. Conclusion : This large monocentric series illustrates the favourable remission rates in pediatric and adolescent CD, and the relatively lower rates of new-onset HH or CHT, especially in younger individuals. Ongoing monitoring post-remission is required, as relapse can occur in one-fourth of cases.

Background and Objective: Pituitary apoplexy (PA) is an acute neuroendocrine emergency caused by haemorrhage in a pituitary adenoma. Although surgery is the traditional approach, emerging evidence supports the safety and efficacy of conservative management. We analysed the data of our patients presenting with acute symptomatic PA to evaluate outcomes of conservative vs. surgical approach. Methods: We retrospectively analysed patients who presented with acute symptomatic pituitary apoplexy (both clinical and radiological) from 01/01/2006 to 12/12/2024 with at least one follow-up visit. We collated data on the clinical symptoms, visual field deficits, cranial nerve palsy, hormonal deficits and imaging characters at presentation, and compared the outcomes between patients managed conservatively vs. those who needed surgical treatment. Results: A total of 101 patients with PA were included, of whom 61 (60.4%) were managed conservatively, and 40 (39.6%) underwent surgery (39 transsphenoidal). Twenty patients (19.8%) had functioning pituitary tumors, while 81 (80.2%) had non-functioning pituitary tumors. Surgically managed patients had significantly higher pituitary apoplexy score (4.0 ± 1.5 vs. 2.1 ± 1.9, P < 0.001), worse visual field impairment (80% vs. 47.5%, P = 0.002) and larger tumour diameter (33.3 vs. 26 mm, P = 0.002) as compared to conservatively managed patients. Headache and hypopituitarism were noted in >90% in both groups, and there was no significant difference. Thirteen patients (21%) managed conservatively had persistent tumour or evidence of tumor growth needing surgery after 1-30 months. At a median follow-up of 46 months, there was no significant difference in pituitary hormonal axis recovery or new hormonal deficiencies between the two groups. Conclusion: Patients with larger tumours, significant visual field defects, and higher PAS scores benefited from surgical management for acute symptomatic PA. Conservative management remains a safe approach for patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms without worsening visual deficits. The long-term endocrine outcomes were comparable between the two approaches.

Background: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogs are the standard treatment for Gonadotropin dependent precious puberty (GDPP). Our aim was to describe anthropometric and metabolic follow-up of GDPP patients after treatment with leuprolide for one year. Methods: Twenty-five patients with GDPP were treated with leuprolide. Their anthropometric and metabolic parameters were evaluated before and after one year of leuprolide treatment. Height-SDS, Weight-SDS and BMI-SDS were calculated as per IAP charts 2015; Waist circumference-SDS as per Khadilkar et al , 2014. Dyslipidemia and risk factors for Metabolic Syndrome (MetS) in children were determined by using the criteria published by Ford et al . Results: This study included 25 children diagnosed with GDPP, with a median age of 7 years; 21 were girls and 4 boys. Most (88%) had primary GDPP, while 5 developed secondary GDPP due to delayed or inadequate treatment of gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty (GIPP). Median bone age was 10 years. At diagnosis, 24% had obesity, 28% had central obesity and dyslipidemia (mainly high triglycerides), and 8% had prediabetes. 20% had two or more MetS risk factors. Following 1 year of Leuprolide injections, we noted a significant reduction in BMI-SDS (0.58 vs 0.98, P = 0.01, median ΔBMI-SDS over 1 year = -0.4) Waist circumference-SDS ( 0.11 vs -0.27, P < 0.001, median ΔWC-SDS over 1 year = - 0.36) and also Waist-height ratio ( 0.5 vs 0.46, P < 0.001, median ΔWHtR-SDS over 1 year = -0.03) in addition to expected reduction in Ht SDS ( 1.55 vs 1.4, P = 0.003, ΔHt-SDS = -0.26). There was also significant reduction in fasting triglycerides (108 vs 96 mg/dl, P = 0.03). Three patients still had obesity by BMI criteria but only two had central obesity and only one persisted having > =1 risk factors for MetS. There was significant correlation between reduction in Triglyceride levels and reduction in WC-SDS ( r = 0.55, P = 0.007). Conclusion: Leuprolide therapy can help reduce central obesity and metabolic risk in children with GDPP.

Background: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH), characterized by deficient GnRH secretion, includes Kallmann syndrome (KS) with anosmia. This study investigates the genetic basis of IHH and explores genotype-phenotype correlations. Significant genetic and clinical heterogeneity is observed in IHH, with autosomal genes playing a key role. Methods: We evaluated 21 patients presenting with IHH. Patients underwent clinical phenotyping, hormonal analysis, and targeted gene sequencing using a clinical exome panel of 40 IHH-related genes. Patients were classified as KS (IHH with anosmia) or normosmic IHH (nIHH). Olfactory bulb imaging was performed in KS patients. Results: The cohort comprised 12 males and 9 females (mean age: 25.6 years). Twelve patients had KS, and 9 had nIHH. Absent/hypoplastic olfactory bulbs/sulci were observed in 7/12 KS patients. Associated anomalies included bimanual synkinesia ( n = 2), renal agenesis ( n = 1), submucosal cleft palate ( n = 1), and other varied findings. Genetic mutations were identified in 17/21 patients (81%). In KS, mutations were found in KAL1 ( n = 3), CHD7 ( n = 3), FGFR1 ( n = 1), PROKR2 ( n = 1), and CCDC141 ( n = 1). In nIHH, mutations were in GnRHR ( n = 2), FGFR1 ( n = 1), KAL1 ( n = 1), HS6ST1 ( n = 1), digenic PROKR2/IL17RD ( n = 1), and homozygous KALL1 deletion ( n = 1). Four patients had no identified mutations. Conclusion: This study confirms the substantial genetic heterogeneity of IHH, with a high mutation detection rate. While clear genotype-phenotype correlations are limited, the phenotypic overlap with CHD7 and KAL1 mutations is reinforced. The novel CCDC141 mutation warrants further investigation in IHH.

Context : 68 Ga-Pentixafor positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) has shown potential in primary aldosteronism (PA) subtyping, but analysis of its diagnostic accuracy based on contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) concordance and PET/CT avidity patterns is lacking. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of 68 Ga-Pentixafor PET/CT for subtyping PA, and to assess its performance based on concordance with CECT and PET/CT avidity patterns. Methods: Clinical, biochemical, radiological, functional imaging, treatment, histopathological and follow-up details of 30 patients with PA who underwent PET/CT over two years at a tertiary centre in India were retrospectively analysed. Diagnostic accuracy of PET/CT for PA subtyping was evaluated in the whole cohort and in subgroups based on CECT-PET/CT concordance and PET/CT avidity patterns. Results: Out of the 30 patients, final subtype classification was achieved in 15 (9 unilateral and 6 bilateral) based on surgical outcomes and/or AVS. PET/CT correctly subtyped 14/15 (93.3%) patients. CECT and PET/CT concordance was seen in 10 patients and PET/CT accuracy was 100% (10/10) in this subgroup. CECT and PET/CT discordance (CECT bilateral and PET/CT unilateral) was seen in 5 patients and PET/CT accuracy in this subgroup was 80% (4/5). PET/CT avidity patterns in the 15 patients having final subtype classification were unilateral avid ( n = 10), bilateral avid ( n = 2), and bilateral non-avid ( n = 3). Diagnostic accuracy of PET/CT was 90% (9/10) in patients with unilateral avidity, and 100% in those with bilateral avidity or non-avidity. Conclusion: Preliminary analysis of CECT-PET/CT scan concordance and PET/CT avidity patterns suggests that PET/CT demonstrates higher accuracy in certain subgroups, potentially guiding the triage for AVS.

Background: The rising incidence of adrenal incidentalomas necessitates non-invasive diagnostic tools. While urine steroid profiling data are abundant, serum liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LCMS/MS) data remain limited. Hence, we aim to study the serum steroid profile by LCMS/MS in adrenal masses, with a focus to distinguish adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) from other adrenal masses. Material and Methods : Patients with a histopathological diagnosis of adrenal masses and preoperative serum 13-steroid panel via LCMS/MS were included. Clinical, biochemical, and radiological data of the ACC group was compared with the non-ACC group. Results: A total of 96 patients (58 females) were included (ACC: 40, Adenoma: 18, Pheochromocytoma: 11, metastases: 4, PBMAH: 9, Myelolipoma: 5, Cyst: 3, Schwanomma/Ganglioneuroma: 3, lymphoma: 3). Symptomatic presentation predominated in both ACC (80%) and non-ACC (67.5%) groups. ACC had a significantly larger diameter (9.85 vs. 3.9 cm, P < 0.001) and a larger number of elevated steroids (2 vs. 0, P < 0.001). Key steroid distinguishing ACC from non-ACC group included: androstenedione (1.36 vs. 0.571 ng/ml, P < 0.001), 11-deoxycortisol (1.88 vs. 0.305 ng/ml, P < 0.001), dehydroepiandrosterone [DHEA] (1.965 vs. 0.680 μg/L, P < 0.001), DHEAS (1780 vs. 354.5 μg/L, P < 0.001), 17OH-progesterone (0.795 vs. 0.470 ng/ml, P = 0.003), and progesterone (0.410 vs 0.12 in women, P 0.004; 0.180 vs 0.09, P 0.031 in men). Additionally, testosterone levels were significantly higher in women with ACC as compared to the non-ACC group (0.44 vs 0.14, P < 0.001). Conclusion: Serum steroid profiling via LCMS/MS is a useful adjunct to distinguish ACC from other adrenal masses.

Background: S aline infusion test (SIT) is used to confirm primary aldosteronism (PA). It involves infusing 2 litres of normal saline over 4 h. Possible adverse effects include poor tolerability, volume overload, increased blood pressure and worsening hypokalemia during SIT. We planned to investigate the diagnostic performance of a short 2 h SIT with 1 litre of saline infusion for confirming PA. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 44 patients with low renin hypertension (Direct Renin Concentration <12 mIU/L and Plasma Aldosterone Concentration (PAC) > 5 ng/dL) who underwent SIT. Blood samples were drawn for aldosterone at baseline, 2 h ( t = 120 min) and 4 h ( t = 240 min) of SIT. Diagnostic performance of short SIT was evaluated. ROC analysis was used to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of aldosterone cut-off values at 2 h to confirm PA. Results: ROC analysis yielded 95.2% specificity and 82.6% sensitivity for a PAC of 6.71 ng/dL at t = 120 to confirm PA and an area under the curve of 0.952 (95% CI [0.898, 1.00], P < 0.001). Almost half (20 out of 44 (45.4%) of the patients did not suppress PAC below 6.71 ng/dL at t = 120. Of them, only 1 (5%) patient suppressed PAC below 5 ng/dL at t = 240. No significant changes in BP and serum potassium were noted at t = 120. Conclusion: A PAC of 6.71 ng/dL at 2 h has high sensitivity and specificity for PA confirmation.

Background: Salivary cortisol measurement offers a non-invasive method to assess adrenal function, reflecting free cortisol levels. Variations in saliva collection techniques, such as passive drooling (PD) and Salivette®(S), may influence cortisol estimates. This study evaluated the comparability of these two methods following stimulation with long-acting porcine ACTH (Acton Prolongatum®), and determined salivary cortisol cut-offs for diagnosing adrenal insufficiency (AI). Methods: In this prospective study conducted at a tertiary care center in South India (2022–2024), 103 subjects (61 AI and 42 normal) underwent an intramuscular Acton Prolongatum® stimulation test (APST). Two-hour post-stimulation, salivary cortisol was collected by both, passive drooling and Salivette® methods, alongside serum cortisol measurement. Salivary cortisol was analyzed using an Electrochemiluminescence Immunoassay (ECLIA). Correlation with serum cortisol, agreement between techniques, and optimal diagnostic cut-offs were assessed. Results: Salivary cortisol values from S and PD methods showed strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.967, P < 0.001. ROC analysis identified optimal salivary cortisol cut-offs for diagnosing AI at a serum cortisol threshold of 19 µg/dL: 1.23 µg/dL (S, sensitivity 95.1%, specificity 92.9%) and 1.04 µg/dL (PD, sensitivity 93%, specificity 91.3%). Bland Altmann analysis showed a mean bias of + 0.14ug/dl (S vs PD) implying that S values were slighty but significantly higher than PV ( P value = 1.2x10 -6 ). Conclusion: Both Salivette® and passive drooling methods reliably reflect serum cortisol after APST and demonstrate excellent diagnostic accuracy for adrenal insufficiency. However, due to minor variations between methods, technique-specific cut-offs should be applied. Salivette® sampling offers operational advantages and has marginally better correlation with serum cortisol.

Background: Primary aldosteronism (PA) is the most common cause of secondary hypertension and is associated with elevated cardiovascular and renal risks independent of blood pressure levels. Adrenal venous sampling (AVS) remains the gold standard for PA subtyping, yet cortisol- based normalization can be confounded by autonomous cortisol secretion, impacting diagnostic accuracy. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of plasma metanephrine normalization compared to cortisol normalization during AVS in patients with PA. Design and Subjects: This was a retrospective analysis of 26 patients with biochemically confirmed PA undergoing AVS. Plasma cortisol and metanephrine were simultaneously measured to assess selectivity and lateralization indices. Both unstimulated and cosyntropin-stimulated AVS protocols were employed. Results: Among 26 patients, 11 patients underwent unstimulated, and 15 underwent stimulated AVS. Bilateral successful cannulation was noted in 96.1% of patients where metanephrine- based selectivity index was used, compared to 84.6% of patients with cortisol-based selectivity index. In 90.9% of patients, the lateralization results were consistent with both cortisol and metanephrine-based indices. Nine patients underwent adrenalectomy; all histopathological analyses confirmed aldosterone-producing adenomas or micronodules immunopositive for CYP11B2, supporting the accuracy of AVS findings. Postoperative outcomes showed complete biochemical success in 75% and clinical success in 25% at three months, aligning with previous reports. Conclusion: Plasma metanephrine normalization during AVS enhances cannulation success rates and diagnostic precision by mitigating the effects of autonomous cortisol secretion. This approach may offer a superior alternative for PA subtyping, potentially improving surgical outcomes and clinical management.

Background: Critical Illness-Related Corticosteroid Insufficiency (CIRCI) is an under-recognized but potentially life-threatening condition characterized by inadequate adrenal response during critical illness, particularly in patients with septic shock. While its pathophysiology involves dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and impaired glucocorticoid responsiveness, Indian data on CIRCI remains sparse. Objectives: This study aimed to assess CIRCI in critically ill Indian patients with shock, evaluate cortisol dynamics through ACTH stimulation, and determine the prognostic utility of Δ max cortisol in predicting mortality. Methods: A prospective observational cohort study was conducted on 272 patients with non-cardiogenic shock admitted to the ICU of a tertiary care center. All patients underwent the 250 mcg Synacthen stimulation test. Baseline cortisol and post-ACTH cortisol levels at 30 and 60 minutes were recorded. Δ max cortisol was defined as the greatest increase from baseline. Clinical outcomes were analyzed in relation to cortisol response, APACHE IV, and SOFA scores. Results: Δ max cortisol was significantly higher in survivors (15.74 ± 11.25 μg/dL) compared to non-survivors (10.08 ± 8.87 μg/dL) ( P < 0.001). A cut-off of ≤8 μg/dL had a sensitivity of 64.8% and specificity of 74.2% in predicting mortality (AUC 0.693). Baseline cortisol paradoxically was higher in non-survivors, likely reflecting adrenal exhaustion. SOFA scores were higher in non-survivors, but APACHE IV failed to differentiate outcomes. CIRCI prevalence was 55.8%, underscoring its clinical relevance. Conclusion: CIRCI is highly prevalent in Indian ICU patients with shock and is strongly associated with increased mortality. Δ max cortisol is a valuable prognostic marker and may guide early corticosteroid therapy. Incorporating dynamic cortisol assessment in ICU protocols may enhance survival outcomes. Further research is warranted to refine diagnostic thresholds and evaluate long-term effects of CIRCI-focused interventions.

Background: Differences of Sex Development (DSD) are congenital conditions with atypical chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomical sex. 46, XY DSD arises due to gonadal dysgenesis or defects in androgen synthesis/action. Limited data exists from Southeast Asia. Methods: An ambispective analysis was conducted on 50 patients with confirmed 46, XY karyotype and clinical features of atypical genitalia, hypospadias, micropenis, non-palpable testes, clitoromegaly, or primary amenorrhea (EMS <11), attending SGPGIMS Endocrine Clinic (2023–2024). Data on clinical features, investigations, diagnosis, sex of rearing and treatment were assessed. Results: Of the 50 patients, 45 had a definitive diagnosis: 23 (51.1%) androgen biosynthetic defects, 12 (26.7%) androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS), 7 (15.6%) partial gonadal dysgenesis (PGD), 2 (4.4%) complete gonadal dysgenesis (CGD), and 1 (2.2%) ovotesticular DSD. Median age at presentation was 31.5 months (IQR: 7.25–138); 27 were reared as males. EMS scores were lowest in androgen synthesis and action defects. Müllerian structures were noted only in ovotesticular DSD. Three patients had pathogenic mutations one each in Androgen receptor, SRD5A2 and HSD17B3 gene respectively. Conclusion: Early recognition of 46, XY DSD supports appropriate gender assignment, hormonal management, and surgical planning. This study highlights the heterogeneous presentation and etiology in a resource-limited setting.

Introduction: Usually DSDs present during infancy or childhood period. However presentation can be delayed until adolescence or early adulthood. We report a series of 6 patients who presented with pubertal virilization and gender dysphoria which revealed underlying 46XYD. Case Presentation: All 6 patients were assigned female sex at birth and reared as girls and ambiguity was not noted by parents at birth. Mean age of presentation was 16 years. All patients presented with Primary amenorrhoea and significant virilization. One patient had mullerian structures in imaging.5 patients had 46 XY karyotype while one had mos 46XY (29) and 45X (21) suggestive of mixed gonadal dysgenesis The most common etiology was 5 alpha reductase deficiency in 2 cases (33.3%), Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome, 17 beta HSD3 deficiency, Mixed gonadal dysgenesis and Partial gonadal dysgenesis in 1 case (16.67%). 4 patients (66.6%) had gender dysphoria and expressed male gender identity and all of them were reassigned male sex while 2 patients (33.3%) wanted to continue as female in which of one of them underwent gonadectomy and the other lost follow up. Genetic analysis was done in 5 cases (83.3%) and mutation was positive in 4 (66.6%) of them. Conclusion: Multidisciplinary approach is essential for diagnosis and management. Genetic analysis helps in confirming or revising the etiological diagnosis. Timely recognition and individualized care are crucial to support gender identity and optimize long term outcomes.

Background: Altered second-to-fourth digit ratio is a recognized biomarker of intrauterine hypogonadism. For assessing fertility potential, scrotal ultrasound is equally important to detect any structural abnormalities. Limited data available in subjects with hypogonadism especially in congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Furthermore, no study has been done to develop predictive AI- model by incorporating these parameters. Methods: In this case-control, observational study 40 CHH and 32 Klinefelter syndrome with age >18 years were included. 148 age-matched healthy males were recruited. XGBoost (1.6.0) Python library and Scikitlearn (1.0.2) were used to develop predictive AI model. Results: The right 2D:4D was significantly higher in CHH and KS than control (0.98 ± 0.03, 0.97 ± 0.03, 0.95 ± 0.03, P < 0.001). The left 2D:4D was also higher in CHH, KS than control (0.97 ± 0.04, 0.97 ± 0.03, 0.95 ± 0.03, P < 0.05). Majority of subjects with hypogonadism had hypoechoic testis. Testicular microlithiasis (TML) was documented in ~30% of CHH and ~70% of KS. Overall head and tail of the epididymis were small in CHH and KS, however, craniocaudal diameter of the head was larger than controls ( P < 0.001). PRAMAAN had sensitivity and specificity to detect male hypogonadism with a sensitivity of 88% and 95% respectively. LH, FSH, testosterone, stretched penile length, digit ratio, TML, height-to-arm span difference were the most contributed variables in the predictive model. Conclusion: The 2D:4D is higher in CHH and KS. There are structural abnormalities in testis and epididymis. The PRAMAAN model is equally sensitive and specific to detect male hypogonadism.

Background: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) is most common endocrine disorder in reproductive age women, with a global prevalence of 20-25%, often considered precursor of metabolic syndrome. Transcriptomic study reveals gene expression changes and disrupted pathways underlying PCOS, but there is limited literature on it. This gap hinders our ability to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying PCOS. Method: A cross-sectional study conducted at IPGMER, Kolkata, including 120 female MBBS students (>18 years). Participants were clinically assessed and classified into PCOS and non-PCOS using Rotterdam criteria. Assessment included clinical history, anthropometry, biochemical and hormonal tests, DXA scan, pelvic ultrasound and fibroscan. Whole blood samples (from PBMC) from PCOS and non-PCOS students were subjected to RNA extraction and sequencing to identify differentially expressed genes. Result: PCOS was diagnosed in 29% of our population, while 29% population was at risk. Among metabolic parameters, on DXA Scan, median body fat percentage was slightly higher in the PCOS group at 41% (36.8-44.4) versus 39% (35.7-43.2) in the non-PCOS group, and among PCOS, Nonobese PCOS had median body fat percentage 40.2 (36.9-43.2), while in Obese PCOS it was 41 (36.9-44.5). These findings were consistent with more impaired metabolic parameters in PCOS (both obese and nonobese) as compared to non-PCOS. Primary analysis from total RNA sequencing showed 1632 genes distinctly expressed in PCOS ( P value <0.05), out of which 312 genes where upregulated (Fold chain >2) and 123 genes were downregulated (Fold chain <-2). Conclusion: The body fat percentage on DXA shows similar results for obese and nonobese PCOS. The distinct transcriptomic profile obtained in our study might help predict onset of PCOS before clinical manifestation and its metabolic associations. This may be further validated by larger cohort.

Background: Ovotesticular Disorder of Sex development (OTDSD) accounts for 3-10% of all DSDs. It is defined by histopathological presence of ovarian tissue containing ovarian follicles and testicular tissue containing seminiferous tubules in the same individual. Worldwide literature including Indian data on genetics of OTDSD is limited. We aim to describe our experience along with genetic testing in these patients. Methods: Retrospective single centre study of patients with histology-proven OTDSD. Clinical, biochemical, imaging, histopathology and genetic details (cytogenetics, FISH for SRY, clinical exome) were recorded. Results: A total of 15 patients with OTDSD were included in our study, majority (8/15) were evaluated in pre pubertal age group, all but one (P14) were reared as males. Genital atypia (male dominant or ambiguous as per Sinnecker in 13) was the common presenting complaint, 14 patients presented with cryptorchidism (8 unilateral). The patient (P14) presented with abdominal pain and primary amenorrhea at 20.7 years. Amongst the 9 male patients for whom pubertal data was available, all developed gynaecomastia, 3 had cyclical hematuria. Karyotype was 46XX in 14 patients and 46XX, XY in one patient. FSH, LH was within the age specified range for all pre pubertal patients. Mean AMH was 28.7 ng/ml (range 23-34) among four pre pubertal males. Imaging and/or Histopathology showed gonadal presentation as lateral (47%) followed by unilateral (40%) and bilateral (13%). All patients had mullerian structures, uterus was present in 13 of our patients. The patient P14 had dysgerminoma arising from ovotestis, no GCNIS was found in other patients undergoing gonadectomy. Clinical exome testing showed no pathogenic variants except one VUS of RSPO1 in one patient; FISH did not detect SRY gene in any patient. Conclusion: In this monocentric study, genetic yield was low and we describe an unusual case of OTDSD with malignancy.

Objective: The diagnosis of adolescent polycystic ovarian disease is based on the presence of menstrual irregularity and clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism. However, the definition of normal testosterone levels remains unclear. Moreover, Liquid Chromatography Mass Spectroscopy (LCMS) is recommended as the standard for steriod measurements. However, normative data for androgen profiling by LCMS for Indian adolescents is not available. Also, serum AMH levels are currently not recommended for the diagnosis of PCOS due to lack of clarity on normal values in adolescents. In this study, we measured serum androgens (testosterone, androstenedione) and AMH and its relation to the menstrual cycle and body mass index in healthy adolescent girls. Design and Setting: Cross-sectional study in North India among girls studying in private schools. Participants: A total of 1068 post-menarcheal girls aged 10-18 years were screened out of which 175 (16.3%) had menstrual irregularity and/or hirsutism. A total of 744 gave consent for blood sampling and 681 apparently healthy girls with regular menstrual cycles were included in this study. Main Outcome Measures: Serum testosterone was measured using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS) and AMH by Beckman-Coulter automated immunoassay. Results: Median testosterone levels rose significantly with age. AMH levels ( n = 441) also varied significantly with age with peak levels at 14-16 years of age. Results were analyzed separately for girls in the first 3 years and > 3 years post-menarche and in follicular, mid-cycle and luteal phases. Testosterone and AMH levels were significantly higher >3 years post menarche compared to the first 3 years (0.338 ng/ml vs 0.287 ng/ml and 4.17 ng/ml vs 3.2 ng/ml, respectively). Testosterone levels were significantly higher during the menstrual cycle in the mid and luteal phase compared to the follicular phase, with median values across the cycles: follicular phase 0.262 ng/ml (range 0.06-0.706), mid-cycle 0.331 ng/ml (range 0.11-0.80), luteal phase 0.309 (range 0.129-0.833). Serum AMH levels correlated with testosterone levels significantly ( P < 0.001). Conclusions: We have generated menstrual phase-specific reference ranges for testosterone (by LC-MS) and AMH in Indian adolescent girls. Our results show that serum testosterone varies significantly across the menstrual cycle with highest levels during mid-cycle and luteal phases whereas AMH levels are stable throughout.

Background: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) presents as parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma. Majority of PHPT patients are asymptomatic but clinical presentation in India is often symptomatic with bone pains, fractures, and nephrolithiasis. While known genetic mutations in MEN1, CASR, and CDC73 account for a portion of syndromic hyperparathyroidism cases, a substantial proportion of PHPT cases remain unexplained. Current diagnostic challenges arise due to overlapping clinical presentations and limitations in preoperative imaging for lesion localization hence the need for improved molecular markers to guide surgical decision-making and therapeutic interventions. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study was conducted at the Department of Endocrinology, IPGMER, Kolkata. Twenty cases of biochemically and/or histologically confirmed PHPT and twenty control subjects undergoing thyroid surgery were recruited. Clinical examination, biochemical investigations, and radiological imaging were performed. DNA was extracted from both tissue and plasma samples and Sanger sequencing done to identify known driver gene mutations. Proteomic profiling was done from plasma to identify protein signatures. Results: Mean preoperative serum calcium and PTH levels were 11.37 ± 0.99 mg/dL and 325.25 ± 297.40 pg/mL respectively; postoperatively they averaged 8.96 ± 1.27 mg/dL and 37.65 ± 39.92 pg/mL respectively. Trimmed Mean ALP was 139.88 ± 34.98 U/L preoperatively and 126.63 ± 29.95 U/L postoperatively. Multiglandular disease noted in four patients. Among patients who underwent DXA, the mean T-scores were −2.45 at the lumbar spine, −1.85 and -1.75 at the right and left femoral necks respectively, and −3.4 at the non-dominant forearm. We identified 120 peptides from hyperplasia group, 108 peptides from adenoma group and 122 peptides from control group. 93 of them were common to all groups. 9 peptides were unique to hyperplasia group, 2 to adenoma group and 14 to control group. Conclusion: This study integrates genomic and proteomic approaches to characterize the molecular landscape of PHPT and thus helps to advance the pathophysiology and preoperative diagnosis of PHPT.

Background: Thalassemia, a common genetic disorder requiring regular transfusions, leads to bone deformities and iron overload. While survival has improved, bone complications remain prevalent. Bone disease is complex, with fractures occurring even with normal BMD. DXA, a 2D assessment tool, has limitations. HR-pQCT offers a 3D view, enhancing bone health evaluation. Aims: This study assessed fracture prevalence, low bone mass, bone microarchitecture, turnover markers, and predictors of low bone mass in transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) patients. Methods: A one-year case-control study at SGPGIMS, Lucknow, included TDT patients over 5 years and matched controls. Patients with conditions or treatments affecting bone mass were excluded. Results: The study included 67 TDT patients and matched controls. 23.8% of TDT patients reported fractures. Low bone mass was significantly higher in TDT patients ( P < 0.05). TBS was lower in cases ( P < 0.01). Volumetric BMD and trabecular number were significantly lower in TDT patients, while trabecular separation was higher. Bone resorption marker cross laps was elevated, and bone formation marker P1NP was lower ( P < 0.001). Endocrine dysfunction includes hypothyroidism (22%), hypocortisolism (4.5%), hypogonadism (46%), hypoparathyroidism (21%), and diabetes (25.4%). Conclusion: Thalassemic osteopathy is often ignored but contributes significantly to morbidity. Early assessment and management are vital. TDT patients exhibit reduced bone mass and altered microarchitecture due to multiple factors.

Background: Hypophosphatasia (HPP) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the ALPL gene, resulting in reduced tissue non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNSALP) activity. This enzymatic deficiency leads to elevated levels of inorganic pyrophosphate, impairing mineralization and causing skeletal and dental abnormalities. Objectives : This study evaluates bone health in adults with genetically confirmed HPP using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), trabecular bone score (TBS), and high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) to identify distinct skeletal characteristics compared to matched apparently healthy controls. Methods : Six adults with ALPL-mutation-confirmed HPP and 30 age, sex, and BMI-matched controls were included. Anthropometric measurements, biochemical markers, and bone turnover markers were assessed. DXA was used to measure bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, and 1/3 radius, while HR-pQCT evaluated volumetric BMD (vBMD) and microarchitecture parameters. Results : Patients with HPP exhibited significantly lower serum ALP levels [21 U/L (18,25)] compared to controls [60 U/L (55,72) P < 0.001]. Bone turnover markers showed reduced levels of CTX (283.0 [241.3, 384.0] vs 232.3 [179.3, 252.0] ng/mL; P = 0.042), while P1NP levels were comparable to those of controls. DXA revealed significantly lower T -scores in the lumbar spine, femoral neck and 1/3 radius, compared to the controls. TBS was also significantly lower in HPP group compared to the controls (1.226 [1.206, 1.266] vs 1.341 [1.287, 1.436]; P = 0.003). HR-pQCT revealed a lower trabecular number (0.881 [0.692–1.176] 1/mm vs. 1.321 [1.198–1.414] 1/mm; P = 0.002), reduced trabecular thickness (0.208 [0.180–0.213] mm vs. 0.221 [0.214–0.243] mm; P = 0.016), increased trabecular spacing (1.131 [0.853–1.449] mm vs. 0.731 [0.642–0.812] mm; P = 0.001), and greater trabecular inhomogeneity, as indicated by a higher Tb.1/N.SD (0.627 [0.353–0.739] 1/mm vs. 0.282 [0.233–0.319] 1/mm; P < 0.001), in the HPP group compared to the controls. Conclusion: Patients with HPP demonstrated significantly lower trabecular vBMD and altered trabecular microarchitecture compared to controls, particularly at the radius. These findings highlight the predilection of trabecular bone involvement in HPP, with the radius being a more sensitive site for detecting early bone microarchitectural changes.

Background: While chronic glucocorticoid (GC) therapy is a well-established risk factor for osteoporotic fractures, there remains lack of validated tools driving consensus for treatment thresholds. Objective: We aimed to develop a novel Machine-learning-model——ASTRA-GO, and to compare its performance with existing guideline-based strategies for fracture risk management in chronic glucocorticoid users. Methods: This was a case-control study incorporating data from patients ( n = 371) aged >40 years, receiving at least 2.5 mg/day of prednisone-equivalent glucocorticoids for > 3-months, with primary outcome being development of new fragility fractures over three-year follow-up (identified through skeletal radiographs). Malignancy and those on anti-osteoporosis therapy were excluded. ASTRA-GO was developed utilizing stacking ensemble model combining Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM with a logistic regression meta-classifier. SHAP and LASSO analysis were done to develop a novel normogram (ASTRA-score) to guide treatment-decision. ASTRA-GO was then validated in a separate cohort ( n = 119) of chronic GC users with similar inclusion criteria. Results: ASTRA-GO showed accuracy of 92% (AUROC 0.88) in detecting new-onset fragility fractures seen in n = 107 (22%) on follow-up. Model-generated normogram (ASTRA-SCORE) for guiding treatment threshold included six weighted-predictors: osteoporosis, cumulative GC dose ≥900 mg over six-months (≥5 mg/day), BMI > 24.5 kg/m 2 , prior fragility fractures, > 60 years age and postmenopausal status. In validation cohort, the ML-derived ASTRA-score demonstrated an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.83, with a sensitivity of 86.0%, specificity of 75.0%. In comparison, ACR treatment threshold had an AUC of 0.71 (sensitivity of 88%, specificity of 46.0%) IOF-ECTS recommendations yielded an AUC of 0.75 (sensitivity of 75.9%, specificity of 54%) while the GC-FRAX threshold had an AUC of 0.76 (sensitivity 84%, specificity 63%) respectively. Conclusion: ASTRA-GO is the first, indigenous AI-enabled real-time tool, offering greater accuracy and specificity than current guideline-recommended thresholds, in identifying patients at elevated risk of chronic glucocorticoid-induced fractures who may benefit from preventive therapy.

Background: Turner Syndrome (TS) is commonly associated with reduced bone mineral density (BMD). According to the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD) guidelines, evaluation of lumbar spine and Total Body Less Head (TBLH) BMD is recommended in pediatric populations, particularly in those with short stature or growth delays, with appropriate height adjustments. While lumbar spine BMD has been well studied in TS, data on total body bone density—especially TBLH and height-adjusted values, remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate TBLH BMD and bone mineral content (BMC) Z-scores, adjusted for height Z-score (HAZ), in Indian girls with TS. Methodology: A total of 85 girls with TS (aged 12–18 years) and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were assessed using the GE LUNAR DXA scanner (operator CV: 1.2%). TBLH BMC and areal BMD, both unadjusted and adjusted for height Z -score, were measured and compared between groups. Results: Compared to controls, girls with TS showed significantly lower unadjusted TBLH BMC (-288.91 ± 97.35 g, P = 0.01) and TBLH BMD (-0.08 ± 0.05 g/cm², P = 0.009). However, after adjusting for height Z -score, no significant differences were observed in TBLH BMC Z -score (-0.016 ± 0.661, P = 0.981) or TBLH BMD Z -score (0.6348 ± 0.999, P = 0.950) between the two groups. Conclusion: When adjusted for height Z -score, TBLH BMC and BMD Z -scores in Indian girls with TS are not significantly different from those of age-matched healthy peers. These findings underscore the importance of appropriate height adjustment in DXA interpretation. Further longitudinal studies are warranted to explore bone health trajectories in this population.

Background: Denosumab is routinely administered every six months to prevent fractures in patients with osteoporosis. However, ethnic and physiological differences may permit safe extension of the dosing interval in certain populations. This study evaluated whether baseline bone turnover markers and body mass index (BMI) could help identify postmenopausal North Indian women with osteoporosis who may safely defer denosumab dosing beyond six months. Methods: In this prospective cohort study, 56 postmenopausal osteoporotic women were enrolled and divided into two groups. The delayed group ( n = 28) received denosumab after more than six months (median: 9.5 months), while the standard group ( n = 28) received it at the routine six-month interval. Baseline assessments included serum beta-C-terminal telopeptide (B-CTX), total procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (total P1NP), BMI, and lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD). Vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) was performed at baseline and at the time of the next injection. Treatment decisions were guided by a BTM protocol using a B-CTX threshold of 300 pg/mL. Patients with B-CTX ≥300 pg/mL received denosumab, while those with levels below this threshold were followed with 6-weekly BTM reassessment until treatment criteria were met. Results: The delayed group had significantly lower BMI (23.29 ± 2.77 vs. 25.59 ± 3.03; P = 0.005) and B-CTX levels (497 vs. 794 pg/mL; P < 0.001), while total P1NP showed a non-significant trend toward lower values ( P = 0.061). Median age was similar between groups (63 vs. 65.5 years; P = 0.588), and the proportion of diabetic patients was comparable. B-CTX ≥497 pg/mL had limited predictive value (AUC = 0.53). No new vertebral fractures were observed in either group. Multivariate logistic regression identified lower BMI (OR = 0.60; P = 0.012) and lower B-CTX (OR = 0.99; P = 0.027) as independent predictors of delayed dosing. Conclusion: Delaying denosumab dosing beyond six months appears safe in low-risk postmenopausal women. Lower baseline B-CTX and BMI may serve as useful indicators for individualized treatment decisions in real-world settings.

Background: Clinical studies assessing the effects of LT4/LT3 combination therapy shows varied data in quality of life (QoL) scores compared to LT4 monotherapy in several meta-analyses with majority of the studies showing insignificant statistical difference. Objective of the study was to clinically assess residual symptoms of hypothyroidism on levothyroxine supplementation in patients who are biochemically euthyroid using validated QoL questionnaire (ThyPRO), to evaluate the effect of combination therapy with levothyroxine (LT4) and liothyronine (LT3), at doses adapted according to TSH-level and correlate the findings with serum T3 levels. Methods: Single-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled cross over study. All patients with Primary hypothyroidism with normal TSH and residual symptoms was evaluated through validated QoL ThyPRO questionnaire.(QoL Score >60-included for study).Baseline→ Placebo & T3 supplementation(3 months)→ Randomised Cross Over →Placebo & T3 supplementation (3 months). Thirty subjects were randomized to LT4 + LT3 group (LT4 + LT3 in the morning ( n = 30) or placebo group (LT4 in the morning- n = 30) in a single blind randomised cross over trial. Pituitary-thyroid axis compensation was assessed after 12 weeks, 24 weeks. Clinical parameters, correlation with T3 levels, quality of life, Patient preference were also evaluated at 12 and 24 weeks. Results: LT4 + LT3 group was treated with mean daily LT3 doses of 5.00 µg, with a mean daily LT4 reduction of 15 µg. Combination treatment required greater dose adjustments than placebo (30% vs 52%, P < 0.001), due to thyroid-stimulating hormone reduction, without hyperthyroidism signs or symptoms. At the end of treatment, the LT4 + placebo group had significantly lower T3/T4 compared to the LT4 + LT3 group (0.10 ± 0.05 vs 0.15 ± 0.08, P < 0.001). Preference for combination therapy was found. Conclusions: Three months of combination therapy with LT3 dose adapted according to TSH-level significantly change quality of life compared to the placebo group (40% decrease in ThyPRO Scores and better QoL), correlated with an increase in the T3/T4 ratio.

Background: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) accounts for 80-85% of thyroid cancer, with aberrant oncogenic pathways including mTOR signalling pathway. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are crucial post-transcriptional regulators involved in various aspects of tumor biology including proliferation, apoptosis and metastasis. We explored expression profile, functional significance, and molecular targets of hsa-miR-99a-5p in PTC, with focus on its regulatory relationship with mTOR, an oncogenic driver in thyroid tumorigenesis. Methods: Expression levels of hsa-miR-99a-5p were evaluated in both formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) PTC tissue samples ( n = 25) and MDA-T32 cell line using qRT-PCR. Functional assays—including cell viability, proliferation, wound healing, colony formation, growth rate, and apoptosis—were performed following transfection with hsa-miR-99a-5p mimics. Various bioinformatic target prediction tools were used to identify its potential downstream target. The mTOR expression was also assessed in FFPE tissues and cell lines via qRT-PCR and immunohistochemistry (IHC), and post-transfection changes were analyzed. Results: The expression of hsa-miR-99a-5p was significantly reduced in PTC and MDA-T32 cells. Functional assays demonstrated that ectopic overexpression of hsa-miR-99a-5p results in reduced cell viability, proliferation, migration, and colony-forming ability, alongside increased apoptosis. mTOR was found to be significantly upregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in PTC tissues and cell line. The transfection with hsa-miR-99a-5p mimics resulted in marked downregulation of mTOR expression, suggesting a functional link between miR-99a-5p and mTOR-mediated tumorigenicity. Conclusion: We conclude that hsa-miR-99a-5p is a tumor-suppressive miRNA in PTC, exerting anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects possibly through direct inhibition of mTOR. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of miR-99a-5p restoration in high grade PTCs.

Background: Intrathyroidal parathyroid adenoma composed exclusively of water-clear cells is an exceedingly rare entity (literature review showed only two such cases have been reported worldwide) that may present with diagnostic challenges. When typical imaging and cytological findings suggest thyroid malignancy with nodal metastasis, such misdiagnosis can lead to extensive surgical intervention. Case presentation: A 35-year-old woman presented with left cervical lymphadenopathy and multiple thyroid nodules. The thyroid function test was normal. Ultrasound of the neck (including thyroid gland) showed multiple thyroid nodules in both left (mainly) and right lobes, of which one nodule in the right lobe was reported as TIRADS 5, while another nodule in the left lobe was assigned as TIRADS 3. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the left cervical lymph node (LN) suggested a metastatic thyroid carcinoma. However, FNAC from multiple thyroid nodules was non-diagnostic for malignancy. FDG PET scan further supported the possibility of a primary thyroid malignancy with secondaries in the left cervical LN. Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormones were normal. Based on these, the patient underwent total thyroidectomy with central and lateral neck dissection. Histopathological examination (HPE) revealed no evidence of malignancy in the thyroid gland or any LNs, including the largest left cervical LN. However, HPE reported a lateral aberrant thyroid in the left cervical LN, a few other LNs, and an intrathyroidal water-clear cell parathyroid adenoma. Immunohistochemistry of the tumor cell expressed CK7, Pax8, GATA3, and chromogranin A positivity, while it was negative for synaptophysin, CAIX, and CD10, suggesting a parathyroid origin. Conclusion: This case highlights an exceedingly rare non-functional intrathyroidal water-clear cell parathyroid adenoma masquerading as metastatic thyroid carcinoma on cytology and imaging. Clinicians and pathologists must remain vigilant about rare diagnostic mimics to prevent over-treatment and ensure appropriate patient management. This is the first case being reported from India.

Objective: To determine an appropriate cut-off of capillary Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) for congenital hypothyroidism. Study design : Cross-sectional. Participants : 174,000 neonates born in different hospitals of Delhi, India, from November 2014 to October 2016. Main Outcome Measures : Correlation between initial and repeat capillary TSH level and subsequent venous free thyroxine (fT4) level. Results: 102 newborns with initial/ repeat capillary TSH level of ≥20 mIU/L ( n = 174) were confirmed to have congenital hypothyroidism at mean (SD) age of 5 (4) days. A good correlation between capillary TSH level and confirmatory venous fT4 level and postnatal age of sampling was obtained (r -0.6, -0.4). The area under the ROC curve (AUC) was 0.81 (95%CI 0.75 to 0.88), indicating referral capillary TSH level of 20 mIU/L to be a good predictor of subsequent high venous TSH level. Conclusion : A cut off of ≥20 mIU/L for capillary TSH screening beyond 24 h of life is optimal in the Indian setting for deciding further recall and workup, keeping a balance between sensitivity and recall rate.

Background: Graves’ disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition, is associated with multiple cardiovascular complications, including pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Although the prevalence of PAH in Graves’ disease is reported to be 35–65%, its pathogenesis and reversibility with antithyroid therapy remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of PAH in newly diagnosed Graves’ disease, assess its reversibility with treatment, and explore associations with thyroid autoantibodies. Methods: Ninety patients with newly diagnosed Graves’ disease were enrolled based on clinical and biochemical evidence of hyperthyroidism and TSH receptor antibody positivity. Baseline assessments included thyroid function tests, anti-TPO and TSH receptor antibodies, and transthoracic echocardiography to measure mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP). PAH was defined as mPAP >20 mmHg. All patients were treated with antithyroid drugs and reassessed by echocardiography three months after achieving Euthyroidism. Results: PAH was present in 43% of patients at baseline. TSH receptor antibody levels, but not anti-TPO antibodies, showed significant correlation with mPAP. After achieving euthyroidism, 87% of patients with baseline PAH demonstrated normalization of pulmonary pressures. A significant reduction in cardiac chamber dimensions was also observed post-treatment. Conclusion: PAH is a common but reversible complication in Graves’ disease, with a strong association with TSH receptor antibody levels. Routine screening for PAH in newly diagnosed Graves’ disease should be considered, as timely treatment can lead to substantial cardiovascular improvement.
