Objective: The diagnosis of adolescent polycystic ovarian disease is based on the presence of menstrual irregularity and clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism. However, the definition of normal testosterone levels remains unclear. Moreover, Liquid Chromatography Mass Spectroscopy (LCMS) is recommended as the standard for steriod measurements. However, normative data for androgen profiling by LCMS for Indian adolescents is not available. Also, serum AMH levels are currently not recommended for the diagnosis of PCOS due to lack of clarity on normal values in adolescents. In this study, we measured serum androgens (testosterone, androstenedione) and AMH and its relation to the menstrual cycle and body mass index in healthy adolescent girls. Design and Setting: Cross-sectional study in North India among girls studying in private schools. Participants: A total of 1068 post-menarcheal girls aged 10-18 years were screened out of which 175 (16.3%) had menstrual irregularity and/or hirsutism. A total of 744 gave consent for blood sampling and 681 apparently healthy girls with regular menstrual cycles were included in this study. Main Outcome Measures: Serum testosterone was measured using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS) and AMH by Beckman-Coulter automated immunoassay. Results: Median testosterone levels rose significantly with age. AMH levels ( n = 441) also varied significantly with age with peak levels at 14-16 years of age. Results were analyzed separately for girls in the first 3 years and > 3 years post-menarche and in follicular, mid-cycle and luteal phases. Testosterone and AMH levels were significantly higher >3 years post menarche compared to the first 3 years (0.338 ng/ml vs 0.287 ng/ml and 4.17 ng/ml vs 3.2 ng/ml, respectively). Testosterone levels were significantly higher during the menstrual cycle in the mid and luteal phase compared to the follicular phase, with median values across the cycles: follicular phase 0.262 ng/ml (range 0.06-0.706), mid-cycle 0.331 ng/ml (range 0.11-0.80), luteal phase 0.309 (range 0.129-0.833). Serum AMH levels correlated with testosterone levels significantly ( P < 0.001). Conclusions: We have generated menstrual phase-specific reference ranges for testosterone (by LC-MS) and AMH in Indian adolescent girls. Our results show that serum testosterone varies significantly across the menstrual cycle with highest levels during mid-cycle and luteal phases whereas AMH levels are stable throughout.

Background: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) presents as parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma. Majority of PHPT patients are asymptomatic but clinical presentation in India is often symptomatic with bone pains, fractures, and nephrolithiasis. While known genetic mutations in MEN1, CASR, and CDC73 account for a portion of syndromic hyperparathyroidism cases, a substantial proportion of PHPT cases remain unexplained. Current diagnostic challenges arise due to overlapping clinical presentations and limitations in preoperative imaging for lesion localization hence the need for improved molecular markers to guide surgical decision-making and therapeutic interventions. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study was conducted at the Department of Endocrinology, IPGMER, Kolkata. Twenty cases of biochemically and/or histologically confirmed PHPT and twenty control subjects undergoing thyroid surgery were recruited. Clinical examination, biochemical investigations, and radiological imaging were performed. DNA was extracted from both tissue and plasma samples and Sanger sequencing done to identify known driver gene mutations. Proteomic profiling was done from plasma to identify protein signatures. Results: Mean preoperative serum calcium and PTH levels were 11.37 ± 0.99 mg/dL and 325.25 ± 297.40 pg/mL respectively; postoperatively they averaged 8.96 ± 1.27 mg/dL and 37.65 ± 39.92 pg/mL respectively. Trimmed Mean ALP was 139.88 ± 34.98 U/L preoperatively and 126.63 ± 29.95 U/L postoperatively. Multiglandular disease noted in four patients. Among patients who underwent DXA, the mean T-scores were −2.45 at the lumbar spine, −1.85 and -1.75 at the right and left femoral necks respectively, and −3.4 at the non-dominant forearm. We identified 120 peptides from hyperplasia group, 108 peptides from adenoma group and 122 peptides from control group. 93 of them were common to all groups. 9 peptides were unique to hyperplasia group, 2 to adenoma group and 14 to control group. Conclusion: This study integrates genomic and proteomic approaches to characterize the molecular landscape of PHPT and thus helps to advance the pathophysiology and preoperative diagnosis of PHPT.

Background: Thalassemia, a common genetic disorder requiring regular transfusions, leads to bone deformities and iron overload. While survival has improved, bone complications remain prevalent. Bone disease is complex, with fractures occurring even with normal BMD. DXA, a 2D assessment tool, has limitations. HR-pQCT offers a 3D view, enhancing bone health evaluation. Aims: This study assessed fracture prevalence, low bone mass, bone microarchitecture, turnover markers, and predictors of low bone mass in transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) patients. Methods: A one-year case-control study at SGPGIMS, Lucknow, included TDT patients over 5 years and matched controls. Patients with conditions or treatments affecting bone mass were excluded. Results: The study included 67 TDT patients and matched controls. 23.8% of TDT patients reported fractures. Low bone mass was significantly higher in TDT patients ( P < 0.05). TBS was lower in cases ( P < 0.01). Volumetric BMD and trabecular number were significantly lower in TDT patients, while trabecular separation was higher. Bone resorption marker cross laps was elevated, and bone formation marker P1NP was lower ( P < 0.001). Endocrine dysfunction includes hypothyroidism (22%), hypocortisolism (4.5%), hypogonadism (46%), hypoparathyroidism (21%), and diabetes (25.4%). Conclusion: Thalassemic osteopathy is often ignored but contributes significantly to morbidity. Early assessment and management are vital. TDT patients exhibit reduced bone mass and altered microarchitecture due to multiple factors.

Background: Hypophosphatasia (HPP) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the ALPL gene, resulting in reduced tissue non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNSALP) activity. This enzymatic deficiency leads to elevated levels of inorganic pyrophosphate, impairing mineralization and causing skeletal and dental abnormalities. Objectives : This study evaluates bone health in adults with genetically confirmed HPP using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), trabecular bone score (TBS), and high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) to identify distinct skeletal characteristics compared to matched apparently healthy controls. Methods : Six adults with ALPL-mutation-confirmed HPP and 30 age, sex, and BMI-matched controls were included. Anthropometric measurements, biochemical markers, and bone turnover markers were assessed. DXA was used to measure bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, and 1/3 radius, while HR-pQCT evaluated volumetric BMD (vBMD) and microarchitecture parameters. Results : Patients with HPP exhibited significantly lower serum ALP levels [21 U/L (18,25)] compared to controls [60 U/L (55,72) P < 0.001]. Bone turnover markers showed reduced levels of CTX (283.0 [241.3, 384.0] vs 232.3 [179.3, 252.0] ng/mL; P = 0.042), while P1NP levels were comparable to those of controls. DXA revealed significantly lower T -scores in the lumbar spine, femoral neck and 1/3 radius, compared to the controls. TBS was also significantly lower in HPP group compared to the controls (1.226 [1.206, 1.266] vs 1.341 [1.287, 1.436]; P = 0.003). HR-pQCT revealed a lower trabecular number (0.881 [0.692–1.176] 1/mm vs. 1.321 [1.198–1.414] 1/mm; P = 0.002), reduced trabecular thickness (0.208 [0.180–0.213] mm vs. 0.221 [0.214–0.243] mm; P = 0.016), increased trabecular spacing (1.131 [0.853–1.449] mm vs. 0.731 [0.642–0.812] mm; P = 0.001), and greater trabecular inhomogeneity, as indicated by a higher Tb.1/N.SD (0.627 [0.353–0.739] 1/mm vs. 0.282 [0.233–0.319] 1/mm; P < 0.001), in the HPP group compared to the controls. Conclusion: Patients with HPP demonstrated significantly lower trabecular vBMD and altered trabecular microarchitecture compared to controls, particularly at the radius. These findings highlight the predilection of trabecular bone involvement in HPP, with the radius being a more sensitive site for detecting early bone microarchitectural changes.

Background: While chronic glucocorticoid (GC) therapy is a well-established risk factor for osteoporotic fractures, there remains lack of validated tools driving consensus for treatment thresholds. Objective: We aimed to develop a novel Machine-learning-model——ASTRA-GO, and to compare its performance with existing guideline-based strategies for fracture risk management in chronic glucocorticoid users. Methods: This was a case-control study incorporating data from patients ( n = 371) aged >40 years, receiving at least 2.5 mg/day of prednisone-equivalent glucocorticoids for > 3-months, with primary outcome being development of new fragility fractures over three-year follow-up (identified through skeletal radiographs). Malignancy and those on anti-osteoporosis therapy were excluded. ASTRA-GO was developed utilizing stacking ensemble model combining Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM with a logistic regression meta-classifier. SHAP and LASSO analysis were done to develop a novel normogram (ASTRA-score) to guide treatment-decision. ASTRA-GO was then validated in a separate cohort ( n = 119) of chronic GC users with similar inclusion criteria. Results: ASTRA-GO showed accuracy of 92% (AUROC 0.88) in detecting new-onset fragility fractures seen in n = 107 (22%) on follow-up. Model-generated normogram (ASTRA-SCORE) for guiding treatment threshold included six weighted-predictors: osteoporosis, cumulative GC dose ≥900 mg over six-months (≥5 mg/day), BMI > 24.5 kg/m 2 , prior fragility fractures, > 60 years age and postmenopausal status. In validation cohort, the ML-derived ASTRA-score demonstrated an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.83, with a sensitivity of 86.0%, specificity of 75.0%. In comparison, ACR treatment threshold had an AUC of 0.71 (sensitivity of 88%, specificity of 46.0%) IOF-ECTS recommendations yielded an AUC of 0.75 (sensitivity of 75.9%, specificity of 54%) while the GC-FRAX threshold had an AUC of 0.76 (sensitivity 84%, specificity 63%) respectively. Conclusion: ASTRA-GO is the first, indigenous AI-enabled real-time tool, offering greater accuracy and specificity than current guideline-recommended thresholds, in identifying patients at elevated risk of chronic glucocorticoid-induced fractures who may benefit from preventive therapy.

Background: Turner Syndrome (TS) is commonly associated with reduced bone mineral density (BMD). According to the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD) guidelines, evaluation of lumbar spine and Total Body Less Head (TBLH) BMD is recommended in pediatric populations, particularly in those with short stature or growth delays, with appropriate height adjustments. While lumbar spine BMD has been well studied in TS, data on total body bone density—especially TBLH and height-adjusted values, remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate TBLH BMD and bone mineral content (BMC) Z-scores, adjusted for height Z-score (HAZ), in Indian girls with TS. Methodology: A total of 85 girls with TS (aged 12–18 years) and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were assessed using the GE LUNAR DXA scanner (operator CV: 1.2%). TBLH BMC and areal BMD, both unadjusted and adjusted for height Z -score, were measured and compared between groups. Results: Compared to controls, girls with TS showed significantly lower unadjusted TBLH BMC (-288.91 ± 97.35 g, P = 0.01) and TBLH BMD (-0.08 ± 0.05 g/cm², P = 0.009). However, after adjusting for height Z -score, no significant differences were observed in TBLH BMC Z -score (-0.016 ± 0.661, P = 0.981) or TBLH BMD Z -score (0.6348 ± 0.999, P = 0.950) between the two groups. Conclusion: When adjusted for height Z -score, TBLH BMC and BMD Z -scores in Indian girls with TS are not significantly different from those of age-matched healthy peers. These findings underscore the importance of appropriate height adjustment in DXA interpretation. Further longitudinal studies are warranted to explore bone health trajectories in this population.

Background: Denosumab is routinely administered every six months to prevent fractures in patients with osteoporosis. However, ethnic and physiological differences may permit safe extension of the dosing interval in certain populations. This study evaluated whether baseline bone turnover markers and body mass index (BMI) could help identify postmenopausal North Indian women with osteoporosis who may safely defer denosumab dosing beyond six months. Methods: In this prospective cohort study, 56 postmenopausal osteoporotic women were enrolled and divided into two groups. The delayed group ( n = 28) received denosumab after more than six months (median: 9.5 months), while the standard group ( n = 28) received it at the routine six-month interval. Baseline assessments included serum beta-C-terminal telopeptide (B-CTX), total procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (total P1NP), BMI, and lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD). Vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) was performed at baseline and at the time of the next injection. Treatment decisions were guided by a BTM protocol using a B-CTX threshold of 300 pg/mL. Patients with B-CTX ≥300 pg/mL received denosumab, while those with levels below this threshold were followed with 6-weekly BTM reassessment until treatment criteria were met. Results: The delayed group had significantly lower BMI (23.29 ± 2.77 vs. 25.59 ± 3.03; P = 0.005) and B-CTX levels (497 vs. 794 pg/mL; P < 0.001), while total P1NP showed a non-significant trend toward lower values ( P = 0.061). Median age was similar between groups (63 vs. 65.5 years; P = 0.588), and the proportion of diabetic patients was comparable. B-CTX ≥497 pg/mL had limited predictive value (AUC = 0.53). No new vertebral fractures were observed in either group. Multivariate logistic regression identified lower BMI (OR = 0.60; P = 0.012) and lower B-CTX (OR = 0.99; P = 0.027) as independent predictors of delayed dosing. Conclusion: Delaying denosumab dosing beyond six months appears safe in low-risk postmenopausal women. Lower baseline B-CTX and BMI may serve as useful indicators for individualized treatment decisions in real-world settings.

Background: Clinical studies assessing the effects of LT4/LT3 combination therapy shows varied data in quality of life (QoL) scores compared to LT4 monotherapy in several meta-analyses with majority of the studies showing insignificant statistical difference. Objective of the study was to clinically assess residual symptoms of hypothyroidism on levothyroxine supplementation in patients who are biochemically euthyroid using validated QoL questionnaire (ThyPRO), to evaluate the effect of combination therapy with levothyroxine (LT4) and liothyronine (LT3), at doses adapted according to TSH-level and correlate the findings with serum T3 levels. Methods: Single-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled cross over study. All patients with Primary hypothyroidism with normal TSH and residual symptoms was evaluated through validated QoL ThyPRO questionnaire.(QoL Score >60-included for study).Baseline→ Placebo & T3 supplementation(3 months)→ Randomised Cross Over →Placebo & T3 supplementation (3 months). Thirty subjects were randomized to LT4 + LT3 group (LT4 + LT3 in the morning ( n = 30) or placebo group (LT4 in the morning- n = 30) in a single blind randomised cross over trial. Pituitary-thyroid axis compensation was assessed after 12 weeks, 24 weeks. Clinical parameters, correlation with T3 levels, quality of life, Patient preference were also evaluated at 12 and 24 weeks. Results: LT4 + LT3 group was treated with mean daily LT3 doses of 5.00 µg, with a mean daily LT4 reduction of 15 µg. Combination treatment required greater dose adjustments than placebo (30% vs 52%, P < 0.001), due to thyroid-stimulating hormone reduction, without hyperthyroidism signs or symptoms. At the end of treatment, the LT4 + placebo group had significantly lower T3/T4 compared to the LT4 + LT3 group (0.10 ± 0.05 vs 0.15 ± 0.08, P < 0.001). Preference for combination therapy was found. Conclusions: Three months of combination therapy with LT3 dose adapted according to TSH-level significantly change quality of life compared to the placebo group (40% decrease in ThyPRO Scores and better QoL), correlated with an increase in the T3/T4 ratio.

Background: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) accounts for 80-85% of thyroid cancer, with aberrant oncogenic pathways including mTOR signalling pathway. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are crucial post-transcriptional regulators involved in various aspects of tumor biology including proliferation, apoptosis and metastasis. We explored expression profile, functional significance, and molecular targets of hsa-miR-99a-5p in PTC, with focus on its regulatory relationship with mTOR, an oncogenic driver in thyroid tumorigenesis. Methods: Expression levels of hsa-miR-99a-5p were evaluated in both formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) PTC tissue samples ( n = 25) and MDA-T32 cell line using qRT-PCR. Functional assays—including cell viability, proliferation, wound healing, colony formation, growth rate, and apoptosis—were performed following transfection with hsa-miR-99a-5p mimics. Various bioinformatic target prediction tools were used to identify its potential downstream target. The mTOR expression was also assessed in FFPE tissues and cell lines via qRT-PCR and immunohistochemistry (IHC), and post-transfection changes were analyzed. Results: The expression of hsa-miR-99a-5p was significantly reduced in PTC and MDA-T32 cells. Functional assays demonstrated that ectopic overexpression of hsa-miR-99a-5p results in reduced cell viability, proliferation, migration, and colony-forming ability, alongside increased apoptosis. mTOR was found to be significantly upregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in PTC tissues and cell line. The transfection with hsa-miR-99a-5p mimics resulted in marked downregulation of mTOR expression, suggesting a functional link between miR-99a-5p and mTOR-mediated tumorigenicity. Conclusion: We conclude that hsa-miR-99a-5p is a tumor-suppressive miRNA in PTC, exerting anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects possibly through direct inhibition of mTOR. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of miR-99a-5p restoration in high grade PTCs.

Background: Intrathyroidal parathyroid adenoma composed exclusively of water-clear cells is an exceedingly rare entity (literature review showed only two such cases have been reported worldwide) that may present with diagnostic challenges. When typical imaging and cytological findings suggest thyroid malignancy with nodal metastasis, such misdiagnosis can lead to extensive surgical intervention. Case presentation: A 35-year-old woman presented with left cervical lymphadenopathy and multiple thyroid nodules. The thyroid function test was normal. Ultrasound of the neck (including thyroid gland) showed multiple thyroid nodules in both left (mainly) and right lobes, of which one nodule in the right lobe was reported as TIRADS 5, while another nodule in the left lobe was assigned as TIRADS 3. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the left cervical lymph node (LN) suggested a metastatic thyroid carcinoma. However, FNAC from multiple thyroid nodules was non-diagnostic for malignancy. FDG PET scan further supported the possibility of a primary thyroid malignancy with secondaries in the left cervical LN. Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormones were normal. Based on these, the patient underwent total thyroidectomy with central and lateral neck dissection. Histopathological examination (HPE) revealed no evidence of malignancy in the thyroid gland or any LNs, including the largest left cervical LN. However, HPE reported a lateral aberrant thyroid in the left cervical LN, a few other LNs, and an intrathyroidal water-clear cell parathyroid adenoma. Immunohistochemistry of the tumor cell expressed CK7, Pax8, GATA3, and chromogranin A positivity, while it was negative for synaptophysin, CAIX, and CD10, suggesting a parathyroid origin. Conclusion: This case highlights an exceedingly rare non-functional intrathyroidal water-clear cell parathyroid adenoma masquerading as metastatic thyroid carcinoma on cytology and imaging. Clinicians and pathologists must remain vigilant about rare diagnostic mimics to prevent over-treatment and ensure appropriate patient management. This is the first case being reported from India.

Objective: To determine an appropriate cut-off of capillary Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) for congenital hypothyroidism. Study design : Cross-sectional. Participants : 174,000 neonates born in different hospitals of Delhi, India, from November 2014 to October 2016. Main Outcome Measures : Correlation between initial and repeat capillary TSH level and subsequent venous free thyroxine (fT4) level. Results: 102 newborns with initial/ repeat capillary TSH level of ≥20 mIU/L ( n = 174) were confirmed to have congenital hypothyroidism at mean (SD) age of 5 (4) days. A good correlation between capillary TSH level and confirmatory venous fT4 level and postnatal age of sampling was obtained (r -0.6, -0.4). The area under the ROC curve (AUC) was 0.81 (95%CI 0.75 to 0.88), indicating referral capillary TSH level of 20 mIU/L to be a good predictor of subsequent high venous TSH level. Conclusion : A cut off of ≥20 mIU/L for capillary TSH screening beyond 24 h of life is optimal in the Indian setting for deciding further recall and workup, keeping a balance between sensitivity and recall rate.

Background: Graves’ disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition, is associated with multiple cardiovascular complications, including pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Although the prevalence of PAH in Graves’ disease is reported to be 35–65%, its pathogenesis and reversibility with antithyroid therapy remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of PAH in newly diagnosed Graves’ disease, assess its reversibility with treatment, and explore associations with thyroid autoantibodies. Methods: Ninety patients with newly diagnosed Graves’ disease were enrolled based on clinical and biochemical evidence of hyperthyroidism and TSH receptor antibody positivity. Baseline assessments included thyroid function tests, anti-TPO and TSH receptor antibodies, and transthoracic echocardiography to measure mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP). PAH was defined as mPAP >20 mmHg. All patients were treated with antithyroid drugs and reassessed by echocardiography three months after achieving Euthyroidism. Results: PAH was present in 43% of patients at baseline. TSH receptor antibody levels, but not anti-TPO antibodies, showed significant correlation with mPAP. After achieving euthyroidism, 87% of patients with baseline PAH demonstrated normalization of pulmonary pressures. A significant reduction in cardiac chamber dimensions was also observed post-treatment. Conclusion: PAH is a common but reversible complication in Graves’ disease, with a strong association with TSH receptor antibody levels. Routine screening for PAH in newly diagnosed Graves’ disease should be considered, as timely treatment can lead to substantial cardiovascular improvement.

Background: Indeterminate thyroid nodules, based on the current Bethesda system, often require diagnostic surgery, risking inappropriate treatment and long-term morbidity in a significant number of patients. While integrating Bethesda and TIRADS scores improves diagnostic yield, subjectivity remains a challenge. Our previous study, which combined Bethesda categories with a TIRADS score ≥7, achieved a sensitivity of 92% but a relatively lower specificity of 74%, highlighting the need for more precise diagnostic approaches. The current study presents a multimodal, AI-driven framework that fuses ultrasound (USG) and molecular cytology raw data to enhance diagnostic precision. Methodology: USG-guided FNAC was performed on 351 nodules. Bethesda and TIRADS scores were documented for 257 and 242 nodules, respectively. Molecular cytology using multiplex immunocytochemistry with Galectin-3 and Wheat Germ Agglutinin (WGA) was performed on 257 samples. U -Net-based models were trained for segmentation of nodules (from USG: 1306 images) and thyroid cell/clusters (from cytology: 495 microscopic images). Features were extracted using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fused using dense layers. Models were trained on 80% of the dataset and validated on the remaining 20%. Results: U -Net achieved the best segmentation for USG nodules (Intersection Over Union, IoU: 0.88). ResNet classification of USG yielded F1 scores of 0.88 for classifying benign and malignant nodules. Cytology segmentation achieved cluster-level IoUs of 0.76 and classification reached an F1 score of 0.85. Early fusion of USG and cytology features achieved 83% test accuracy. Late fusion using patient-level probability scores yielded 84.2% sensitivity and 96% specificity (AUC: 0.91). Adding Bethesda and TIRAD parameters further improved diagnostic performance (Sensitivity/Specificity: 95%, AUC: 0.99; benign: 19 and malignant: 23). Conclusion: This multimodal AI model demonstrates robust performance in stratifying thyroid nodules and holds strong potential to guide clinical decision-making in indeterminate cases improving better triaging of thyroid nodules

Background: Renal tubular disorders (renal tubulopathies) are an area of enigma for clinicians. Accurate diagnosis requires high index of clinical suspicion and thorough biochemical evaluation of serum and urine parameters. Most of these disorders have a genetic defect in ion channels along the various nephron segments. Demographic and epidemiological observations have revealed that there are certain pockets of West Bengal where these diseases are more prevalent-an area of significance not yet studied. It is hypothesized by clinicians that a second-hit in the form of an environmental contaminant (in soil/water) could be the culprit behind such demographic clustering. For example, distal RTA is endemic in certain parts of the world, as reported in the resident population (LaoThai) of the northeast region of Thailand. Therefore, our study aimed to find the various genetic defects responsible for renal tubular disorders as well as to search for the presence of heavy metal contamination (if any) [literature evidences showing that heavy metals are tubulo-toxic] around residences of patients of renal tubular disorders in the pan Gangetic and Rarh regions of West Bengal, from where maximum such cases have been found. Methods: Hospital based (MCH) observational cross-sectional study. 22 patients of diagnosed renal tubulopathies presenting from southern Bengal were taken. Patients of thyrotoxicosis, uncontrolled diabetes, CCF, CLD, CKD due to other aetiologies, patients on nephrotoxic drugs were excluded. Genetic analysis was done by Whole Exome Sequencing. Determination of heavy metals in drinking water and soil was done by inductively coupled plasma—optical emission spectrometry [spectrometric technique used to determine trace elements in aqueous solutions]. Results: Genetic analysis of 18 out of 22 patients have been done till abstract submission (the rest is expected to be available soon). The number of patients having heterozygous non-pathogenic mutation is significant which raises the possibility of a “second hit” phenomenon, hypothesized here as environmental heavy metals. Samples of soil and water for heavy metal estimation have been sent (reports pending). Conclusion: A likely environmental insult exists for clinical occurrence of renal tubulopathies that explains the aforesaid demographic clustering.

Introduction: Evaluating the impact of gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) on bone health in transgender individuals is essential to prevent skeletal complications. This study assessed changes in bone mineral density (BMD) and bone turnover markers before and after one year of GAHT in gender-incongruent individuals. Methods: This cohort study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital’s Endocrinology department. Participants initiating GAHT, regardless of prior gender-affirming surgery, were enrolled based on specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. BMD at the lumbar spine (LS) and femoral neck (FN), along with bone turnover markers—propeptide of type I procollagen (P1NP) and C-terminal telopeptide of type 1 collagen (β-CTX), were measured at baseline and after one year. Joint flexibility was assessed using shoulder stretch and sit-and-reach tests at both time points. Results: 60 transgender individuals (24 transmen; 26 transwomen) were enrolled; 14 transwomen and 8 transmen were followed for one year. Mean age was 26.69 ± 5.8 years for transwomen and 26.58 ± 4.8 years for transmen. After one year, FN BMD significantly decreased in transwomen (mean difference: -0.02 ± 0.2, P = 0.004). No significant BMD changes were noted in transmen at LS ( P = 0.55) or FN ( P = 0.25). P1NP significantly decreased in transwomen from 69.76 ng/ml to 30.44 ng/ml (mean difference = 39.3, P = 0.01), while β-CTX, joint flexibility scores showed no significant changes in either group. Conclusion: Transwomen showed a decline in FN BMD and P1NP levels after one year of GAHT, suggesting a higher long-term risk of bone loss that warrants further follow-up.

Introduction: NFHS is an extensive, multi-round survey that is carried out across India in a typical household sample. Since its initial administration in 1992–1993, six rounds of survey have been carried out. Aim: To assess the secular Trends in adult height and variables (gender, age, type of residence and diet) affecting it in India. Method: A cross-sectional, observational study using NFHS data of NFHS-2 (1998-1999), NFHS-3 (2005-2006), NFHS-4 (2015–2016) and NFHS-5 (2019–2021) in a nationally representative sample of adult male (aged 20 to 54 years) and female (aged 20 to 49 years) was used. A total of 14,89,666 out of 28,47,943 data of both males and females were used for this analysis of all NFHS. Results: Analysis included 14,89,666 subjects (Male - 231610; 15.5%, Female – 1258056; 84.5%) with mean age of 34.0 ± 9.2 years (Males - 34.7 ± 9.7 years and Females - 33.1 ± 8.4 years). The height of urban dwellers (164.5 ± 6.9, 152.7 ± 5.95 P -value <0.001) is higher than that of rural residents (163.3 ± 7.02, 152 ± 6.0, P -value < 0.001) for both males and females. From NFHS-3 to NFHS-5 there is a decrease of 1.6 cm in adult male height and from NFHS-2 to NFHS-5 there is an improvement of 0.7 cm in adult non-pregnant female height. (Tabulated below). The Regional Trend of adult height shows that North Indian male and female has better Height trend in comparison to other regions (overall; Male - 166 ± 6.94 and Female - 154.6 ± 5.89), NFHS-2 (Female - 153.6 ± 5.66), NFHS-3 (Male - 166.8 ± 6.77 and Female - 154.1 ± 5.91), NFHS-4 (Male - 166.3 ± 6.80 and Female - 154.6 ± 5.76), NFHS-5 (Male - 165.4 ± 7.11 and Female - 154.7 ± 6.02). Conclusion: The trend shows that adult males in India are getting shorter on average. However, there is an improvement in adult female height. Despite heredity, non-genetic factors like social and environmental effects have a significant impact on adult height.

Background : Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) is a rare ciliopathy with multisystem involvement and phenotypic variability, including obesity, retinal dystrophy, hypogonadism, and renal anomalies. Over 20 genes are linked to BBS, but genotype-phenotype correlations remain unclear. Recent meta-analyses reveal gene-specific clinical variability, but Indian data remain scarce. This study addresses the need for population-specific insights by exploring genotype-phenotype associations in BBS patients from a single tertiary center in India. Objective was to establish genotype-phenotype correlations in BBS and identify phenotypic patterns associated with common BBS gene mutations. Methods : In this cross-sectional study, individuals over one year of age diagnosed with Bardet-Biedl syndrome based on Beales criteria were recruited. Whole exome sequencing was performed, and those with incomplete medical records were excluded from the analysis. Results : 15 patients suspected of BBS were screened; after excluding four due to incomplete records, two with Prader-Willi syndrome, and two due to familial duplication, seven index patients (5 males, 2 females) were included for genotype-phenotype correlation. Median age at diagnosis was 14 years (range: 3–41). Parental consanguinity was present in six cases. Most common mutations were identified in BBS10 (3/7) followed by BBS2 (2/7), BBS9 (1/7), and BBS12 (1/7). Obesity presented in 100% of patients, retinal dystrophy and polydactyly in 85.7%, genital abnormalities (mainly hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) in 71.4%, cognitive impairment in 57.1%, and renal anomalies in 28.6%. Minor features included dental anomalies (71.4%) and speech/developmental delays and insulin resistance (57.1%). BBS10 mutations were most frequent and showed consistent association with obesity, polydactyly, and developmental/speech delay. BBS2 mutations were linked with cognitive impairment and retinal dystrophy. BBS9 patient had multisystem involvement, including seizures and renal/genital anomalies. BBS12 patient had a milder phenotype. Conclusions : These results emphasize the phenotypic diversity of BBS and identify BBS10 as the most frequent genotype, showing a strong association with core clinical features.

Background: Insulinoma is a rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causing endogenous hyper-insulinemic hypoglycemia. The gold standard 72-h diagnostic fast is cumbersome and requires admission. Supervised ultra-short fasting test in outpatient department (OPD) can help confirm the diagnosis in selected groups of patients. Methods: We report three cases of Insulinoma presenting with hypoglycemic unawareness. The test was done in the Endocrinology OPD with Department of Biochemistry and Emergency medicine informed one day prior to test. The test was started after a light meal early in the morning and no meal advised for 6-8 hrs thereafter. Blood glucose was checked every 30 min by the patient attendant until they reached OPD and subsequently every 5-15 min by the physician in OPD. Critical samples were collected when the blood glucose was 40 mg% or less. Results: All three female patients (54, 35, and 24 years) were obese with normal Anti-Insulin autoantibody level. Test endpoint attained 2 hrs after the morning meal in patient 1 and 2, while it took 7 hrs for patient 3. During the fast, blood glucose levels dropped to 26-35 mg/dL, with inappropriately elevated insulin (37.7, 27.6 and 17.7 μIU/mL) and C-peptide levels (5.6, 4.6 and 3.2 ng/mL). Blood ketone levels were low (0.01-0.02 nmol/L). Cortisol and growth hormone responses to hypoglycemia were blunted. Imaging studies localized pancreatic tumors: 1.5 cm (tail), 1.8 cm (tail), and 1.7 cm (head) in patient 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Conclusion: Supervised ultrashort diagnostic fast in OPD can be helpful in subgroup of Insulinoma patients.

Background: Isolated growth hormone deficiency (IGHD) may be congenital or acquired. Genetic forms of growth hormone deficiency may occur as IGHD or as a component of multiple pituitary hormone deficiency. This study aimed to look at the novel genetic mutations and its clinical implications in IGHD . Methods: Patients with IGHD were diagnosed as per GHRS, 2000 criteria using anthropometry, IGF-1 and GH-stimulation tests with Clonidine and/or Glucagon. MRI pituitary and whole exome sequencing (WES) was done for all and pathogenicity of mutations analyzed using Illumina-NGS-platform. We divided the cohort into 3 groups (those with mutations in GHRHR/GH gene [Group A, n = 8], those with pathogenic mutations in genes related to bone/cartilage formation [Group B, n = 9] and negative for mutations [Group C, n = 9]. Results: A total of 29 subjects with IGHD were included, median age 11 years, M = 17, F = 12, median height-SDS -3.7, median IGF-1-SDS -1.28. Hypoplastic pituitary gland was seen in 7 subjects (24.1%). WES revealed known and novel pathogenic mutations in GHRHR & GH genes ( n = 5 and 1 respectively). Notably 9 patients had pathogenic mutations in genes implicated in collagen or cartilage development & associated with metaphyseal/epiphyseal dysplasias ( COL10A1, BMPR1B, FLNB, MKS1, TBX2, PDE3A, COL9A2 & MYH8 ). Patients in Group A had delayed presentation (13 vs 10.8 vs 8.9 years). There was no difference in height SDS or IGF-1 between the groups but the GH max on stimulation tests were significantly lower in Group A (0.92 vs 2.5 vs 2.2, P = 0.04). Notably, those in Group B had the highest first year height velocity (10.5 cm) followed by Group A (9.03 cm), and Group C (8.8 cm) ( P = 0.05). Highest proportion of hypoplastic pituitary/empty sella was noted in Group A ( n = 3, 50%) followed by Group C ( n = 3, 37.5%). Conclusion: We report novel genetic mutations in patients with IGHD. The link between genes associated with epi/metaphyseal dysplasia and GHD need exploration but GH therapy leads to significant height improvement in them.
